title: Meet the 22-year-old candidate eyeing history in key swing state as Gen Z embraces conservatism: 'Step up'
excerpt:
Iowa House candidate Dillon Fillion told Fox News Digital that Gen Z is embracing conservatism and laid out his plan to win the swing district in Scott County.

From delivering pizzas to running for a...
body_text:
Iowa House candidate Dillon Fillion told Fox News Digital that Gen Z is embracing conservatism and laid out his plan to win the swing district in Scott County.

From delivering pizzas to running for an Iowa House seat, 22-year-old Dillon Fillion hopes to make history in his swing district and inspire Gen Z to embrace conservatism, which he says he's already seeing on the ground.

Fillion, believed to be the youngest candidate ever to seek office in Scott County, spoke to Fox News Digital about his ambitions to cut property taxes, boost police funding, give parents more say in their children’s education and draw Gen Z to the polls.

"I think people are very excited that a young person is running because they see a lot of these old people running for office, no offense to them, but people wanna see some fresh new faces and I think it's time for my generation to step up," Fillion said.

Before launching his bid for the Iowa House, Fillion decided to take a gap year from Scott Community College, where he is pursuing a criminal justice degree. He currently works as a Domino’s delivery driver while hitting the campaign trail, which he described as juggling "two full-time jobs."

MEDIA NARRATIVE PREDICTING BLUE WAVE IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE NOT MESHING WITH LOCAL REPUBLICANS: 'FIRED UP'

Iowa House candidate Dillon Fillion, 22, is running to represent the state’s 81st House District. (Dillon Fillion for Iowa House/Scott Morgan for The Washington Post via Getty Images)

"Basically, I do a full-time job as well as campaigning," he said.

But campaigning wasn’t always Fillion’s vision. A lifelong hockey fan, he said his initial dream was to play professionally before stepping into politics.

Fillion said he became interested in politics in 2019 after seeing Democrats accuse President Donald Trump of colluding with Russia, saying he found it "weird" they were "calling our president a lot of weird, untrue things." From there, he said he went down a "rabbit hole" researching what he described as corruption within the Democratic Party, which he found "baffling and shocking."

"I just couldn't stand back and just watch all this stuff happen, and I decided to get involved," he said.

"Keep Iowa Great!" is the slogan Fillion has plastered across campaign signs and merchandise as he works to win over Iowa voters. One of three siblings, Fillion had an upbringing "grounded in Christian family values, a strong work ethic, and the perseverance to stand by his principles no matter the challenge," according to his campaign website.

Fillion credited Charlie Kirk with helping young men like him "find a purpose" and turn to conservative principles.

"The men in my generation are really conservative. They admire conservative principles. I think Charlie Kirk really helped with the young men in my generation in regard to finding a purpose in life. And I think that's really helped a lot of men in my generation," Fillion said. "I do think my generation is going in the right direction in regard to conservatism. It's just, I think my generation needs to turn out more in our elections."

LIZ PEEK: HASAN PIKER EXPOSES DEMOCRATS' DESPERATION TO WIN BACK YOUNG MEN

Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk spoke during his "American Comeback Tour" at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025, in Orem, Utah. Kirk was fatally shot while appearing at the event. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)

Fillion will challenge incumbent Democratic state Rep. Daniel Gosa for a seat representing Iowa's 81st House District. Fillion says he finally has the opportunity to "carry the ball down the field" in his district and is calling for a leadership overhaul.

"I wouldn't be in this race if I didn't think I could win it," he said. "However, my Democrat opponent does not stand up for the things that this district cares about."

Among Fillion’s most high-profile endorsements are Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and Iowa House Majority Leader Bobby Kaufmann, according to his campaign website.

DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE

Senator Rick Scott, a Republican from Florida, in the Senate Subway during a vote at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Friday, March 14, 2025. (Allison Robbert/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

One of Fillion’s top priorities is eliminating property taxes completely. His campaign website said if that isn’t "immediately achievable," Fillion will work to lower taxes as much as possible.

"I wanna keep Iowa number one in affordability," he said.

Crime and education are also on Fillion’s mind, and he told Fox News Digital those will be two of his top priorities if elected in November.

"When I get into that legislature, I will be introducing a constitutional amendment for the Back the Blue Act to make sure our police are protected so they can do their job correctly," Fillion said. "And I will continue to empower parents and teachers in our kids' education, because parents should be the forefront of your kids' education, not the government."

He said his ultimate goal is to make Iowa "the number one state to live, work, and raise a family."

With voters preparing to head to the polls in November, Fillion said his campaign aims to spread more optimism and show people that Gen Z wants to make the world a better place.

"I just want our country to know that there are people in my generation that are doing everything they can to try and save this country," he said.

Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: Biden-appointed judge deals Trump another sanctuary city defeat in major immigration fight
excerpt: New York City sanctuary laws are upheld after a federal judge dismisses a Department of Justice lawsuit, drawing sharp criticism from Joe Abraham, whose daughter Katie was killed in a hit-and-run cras...
body_text:
New York City sanctuary laws are upheld after a federal judge dismisses a Department of Justice lawsuit, drawing sharp criticism from Joe Abraham, whose daughter Katie was killed in a hit-and-run crash. Meanwhile, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul deflects questions on migrant crime during a gubernatorial debate.

A Biden-appointed judge dealt the Trump administration another legal blow Thursday, tossing its lawsuit seeking to upend New York City’s sanctuary policies after ruling that the Justice Department’s arguments amounted to a "backdoor around the Tenth Amendment."

The Trump administration sued New York City in July 2025, alleging that its sanctuary laws unlawfully hinder federal immigration enforcement by restricting local law enforcement’s cooperation with federal authorities.

The New York City case is one of more than two dozen lawsuits the Trump administration has filed against state and local jurisdictions over sanctuary and related policies restricting cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

But U.S. District Judge Ramón E. Reyes Jr. ruled that the federal government lacked standing to challenge New York City’s restrictions on honoring ICE detainers and rejected the Justice Department’s claims that the city’s sanctuary policies are preempted by federal law.

MAMDANI BLASTS FEDS FOR WAGING 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE AND TERROR' AGAINST NYC'S IMMIGRANTS

Mayor of New York Zohran Mamdani speaks during a press conference at Middle Collegiate Church in New York City on March 19, 2026. (Leonardo Munoz/AFP via Getty Images)

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani celebrated the ruling in a Friday post on X, accusing the administration of attempting to turn city employees into immigration enforcement agents.

"The federal government tried to turn our public servants into deportation agents and force New York City to carry out ICE’s cruel agenda. Today, a federal court rejected that effort and upheld our laws. Every New Yorker deserves to seek help from their city without fear of being targeted for deportation. We will stand by our immigrant neighbors, defend our laws and protect the promise that this city belongs to all of us," Mamdani wrote.

Reyes found the administration lacked standing because striking down the city’s restrictions would not remedy its alleged harm because separate state laws restricting cooperation would remain in place.

But Abhishek Kambli, a former federal prosecutor and current partner at Holtzman Vogel, disputed that reasoning, arguing that the city's laws independently harm the federal government's authority regardless of whether similar state restrictions exist.

"The sovereign harm is done just by the fact that New York City has the law in the books, no matter what other factors prevent practical application of the United States's position," Kambli told Fox News Digital.

FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS NEW YORK LAW BANNING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS

Reyes also rejected the Justice Department's argument that New York City's sanctuary policies are overridden by federal immigration law.

"Even if the United States has standing — and it does not — its preemption claims fail," Reyes wrote. "All of the United States’ preemption claims — express, conflict and field — fail because the relevant federal statutes do not regulate private actors."

Dozens of immigrants are detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents inside the Federal Plaza courthouse in New York City on Thursday, June 26, following their legal proceedings. The arrests, which took place shortly after court appearances, have sparked criticism from immigrant rights advocates, who say courthouse enforcement undermines due process and deters community members from seeking legal protection. (Lokman Vural Elibol/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The judge pointed to the Tenth Amendment's anti-commandeering doctrine, which prevents the federal government from forcing state and local governments to use their own officials and resources to administer federal programs.

"If states cannot remain free to control their agencies and employees to resist federal immigration enforcement, which is within states’ constitutional prerogatives, the Tenth Amendment anticommandeering doctrine means nothing," Reyes wrote.

Kambli, however, argued that Reyes misinterpreted the distinction between forcing local governments to assist federal immigration enforcement and preventing them from actively obstructing it.

"Really what the 10th Amendment anti-commandeering means is you can't force states to go from doing nothing to affirmatively assisting. What these statutes are doing is basically preventing states from actively obstructing federal immigration enforcement," Kambli said.

He argued that the Justice Department was not seeking to force New York City officials to carry out federal immigration enforcement, but instead to prevent local laws from interfering with federal authorities' ability to enforce immigration law.

"That's different from the federal government saying a state or a city is required to actively assist ICE in operations," Kambli said.

President Donald Trump arrives to speak during a campaign rally at Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center in Wasilla, Alaska, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images)

HUNDREDS OF JAILED ILLEGAL ALIENS RELEASED BACK ONTO BLUE-STATE STREETS DESPITE ICE DETAINERS, RECORDS SHOW

The Justice Department also argued that New York City's sanctuary policies went beyond simply refusing to assist federal authorities by restricting information-sharing with ICE that is protected under federal law. The administration additionally claimed that the city unfairly singled out federal immigration officials for restrictions that did not apply to other law enforcement agencies.

Reyes, however, found that federal information-sharing protections apply specifically to information about an individual's citizenship or immigration status and do not require local governments to provide ICE with broader details, such as a person's release date or whereabouts.

"The United States’ assertion that information regarding release dates and custody status is information regarding immigration or citizenship status is contrary to law," Reyes wrote.

Kambli, however, argued that the distinction over what information is being withheld misses the greater issue at hand.

"The issue is mainly whether any state or locality that prohibits cooperation is preempted by federal law, regardless of what the information is," Kambli said.

The ruling marks the latest setback for the Trump administration's efforts to challenge sanctuary policies in federal court, following dismissals of similar lawsuits involving Boston, Los Angeles and Minnesota.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: All the president’s women: a familiar downward trajectory in Trump’s cabinet
excerpt:
Half of Trump’s female cabinet officials have been replaced by men, while men facing misconduct allegations remain

Donald Trump is not, by any measure, a feminist. He has said so himself. But the pre...
body_text:
Half of Trump’s female cabinet officials have been replaced by men, while men facing misconduct allegations remain

Donald Trump is not, by any measure, a feminist. He has said so himself. But the president has often pointed to his hiring and promoting of women in an attempt to stave off criticism of both his policies and personal conduct over the years.

During his second term, however, there is one common characteristic among most of those who have departed the Trump administration.

In the space of just a few months, half of his eight female cabinet officials have either resigned or been fired. All have been replaced by men. Several other women in his administration have also departed, whether voluntarily or involuntarily.

On Friday, Trump was forced to deny reports that he was considering replacing Susie Wiles, his White House chief of staff, and the first woman to do the job. “She’s gonna be here for a long time,” he claimed.

Numerous top male officials, meanwhile, from Trump’s defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who has on multiple occasions courted global condemnation, to the widely ridiculed FBI director Kash Patel, have survived intense scrutiny and repeated calls for their resignation – and yet remain in post.

The latest female casualty was White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, who was fired on Friday just five days into the role. After a rocky start to her tenure, sparked by a widely panned first White House press briefing on Tuesday, she had also faced questions over her legal credentials after admitting she did not pass the bar exam. The ensuing semantics battle over whether or not she is a lawyer, or an attorney, placed her in a pickle – even with the rightwing cable network Fox News.

Zacharia had taken over from Karoline Leavitt, who said in August that she had chosen to resign from the role after 20 months so she could spend more time with her young family.

In terms of firings, the first domino to fall was former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem, who was the face of Trump’s mass deportation campaign until she was unceremoniously sacked on 5 March. Her tenure was plagued by controversy, in large part amid national uproar over federal immigration enforcement operations that killed two US citizens in Minneapolis (one of whom Noem called a “domestic terrorist”, with no evidence), and coincided with a sharp decline in national support for Trump’s immigration agenda.

Her suggestion at a congressional hearing in March that Trump had known about her decision to approve a contract for a $220m ad campaign to encourage immigrants to “self-deport” – which prominently featured Noem on horseback – reportedly left Trump “pissed” and appeared to be the straw that broke the camel’s back. There had also been scrutiny of general leadership failures under Noem, as well as questions the influence of her adviser, Corey Lewandowski, who also left his role when she was ousted.

Noem was repurposed as special envoy to the so-called “Shield of the Americas” coalition and, after that arrangement expired last month, is now serving in a vaguely defined advisory role. She was succeeded as DHS secretary by Markwayne Mullin.

Next fell former attorney general and Trump loyalist Pam Bondi, who was pushed out in April after a turbulent 14 months that saw the president increasingly frustrated over her mishandling of the Department of Justice’s long-awaited release of the Epstein files. The Epstein issue became a huge political liability for Trump and infuriated his Maga base, and he also felt that Bondi had failed to sufficiently prosecute his political enemies.

Bondi revealed a month after she was ousted that she had been diagnosed with thyroid cancer. Her deputy, Todd Blanche, assumed the role in August.

It’s worth noting that commerce secretary Howard Lutnick faced public scrutiny after details emerged surrounding his past ties to Jeffrey Epstein and visits to his private island emerged. By contrast, the White House supported him after Democrats called for his resignation.

Also in April, former labor secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer stepped down after a Department of Labor inspector general investigation led to a series of allegations of misconduct, including having an affair with a subordinate and drinking alcohol on the job. She was replaced by Keith Sonderling.

Kash Patel has also been alleged to have been intoxicated or absent on the job. He has denied these allegations, and remains FBI director.

A month later, in May, Tulsi Gabbard resigned from her position as Trump’s national intelligence director.

While she officially cited her husband’s rare cancer diagnosis, Gabbard was reportedly forced out after a tumultuous stint in which she was largely sidelined as Trump launched attacks on Venezuela and Iran. She had previously testified to Congress that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon.

Gabbard was replaced on an acting basis by Bill Pulte, a Trump loyalist with no previous experience in the intelligence sphere, and eventually by Jay Clayton.

Earlier this week, the Trump administration asked longtime Trump ally Kimberly Guilfoyle to step down from her position as US ambassador to Greece after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials.

The only senior male official to have been somewhat punished by Trump since his return to office is Mike Waltz. The then-national security adviser was fired in May last year after inadvertently adding a journalist to a Signal group chat in which Hegseth disclosed secret war plans.

Waltz had been on thin ice with Trump for a while, and the president was reportedly annoyed by Waltz’s hawkish stance on Iran. Signalgate merely sealed his fate.

But he didn’t disappear to some obscure advisory role; Waltz was nominated to the position of US ambassador to the United Nations. Hegseth, meanwhile, was allowed to ride out the controversy and – several controversies later, including allegations of war crimes – remains in post.

Democrats have highlighted the double standard that Trump only seems to fire women in his administration – even those who are ultra-loyal to him, and decidedly less incompetent than some of their male colleagues.

“If you’re a man in the Trump administration, it seems that they reward misconduct,” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the Democratic congresswoman, observed in April.

“I wouldn’t say I’m a feminist,” Trump said in a 2018 interview. “I mean, I think that would be, maybe, going too far. I’m for women. I’m for men. I’m for everyone.”

title: Honeybees are barging aside wild pollinators in hunt for pollen and nectar, study finds
excerpt:
As a surge in beekeepers has lead to increased numbers of honeybees, researchers record them pushing bumblebees and other rival species away from flowers

Honeybees are outcompeting wild pollinators f...
body_text:
As a surge in beekeepers has lead to increased numbers of honeybees, researchers record them pushing bumblebees and other rival species away from flowers

Honeybees are outcompeting wild pollinators for resources by aggressively bumping into them and chasing them away from flowers, research has shown.

The study, by researchers from Anglia Ruskin University, found that areas where there were higher concentrations of honeybees had fewer wild pollinators, such as bumblebees, solitary bees and hoverflies.

Honeybees were also most likely to instigate, and win, competitive interactions, pushing out rivals to collect more pollen and nectar.

The number of managed bees has risen in the UK, as campaigns to “save the bees” resonate with the public, leading to a boom in hobbyists setting up beehives. The number of registered beekeepers has more than doubled, from 19,000 in 2010 to 47,000 in 2025, according to the National Bee Unit.

However, there are growing concerns that this growth in managed honeybees is harming other, wild, pollinators including bumblebees, by increasing competition for food and passing on diseases, especially in areas where there are fewer flowers or an especially high density of hives.

To better understand the nature of this competition, the study in Cambridgeshire observed pollinators over a two-year period as they foraged on bramble and ivy in areas close to honeybee colonies. The study documented the outcomes of 300 interactions between flower visitors from five groups: honeybees, bumblebees, solitary bees, hoverflies and “other”, which included types of flower-visiting and pollinating flies, butterflies, beetles and wasps.

In each interaction, the study noted where an individual “won”, by gaining access to a resource, “lost”, or if a resource was shared. Honeybees won in most of the encounters across both plant species.

Past research has suggested that honeybees outcompete other pollinators indirectly, by taking up resources. However, the Cambridgeshire study provides evidence that they are posing a more direct form of competition, known as “interference competition”, where a species might attack or chase others away.

“That’s important because, of course, it means that the wild pollinators are facing a challenge from both those types of competition from honeybees,” said Victoria Buckle, lead author of the study and a PhD researcher at Anglia Ruskin University.

Honeybees were actively avoided by other flower visitors in 28.4% of interactions on bramble and 35.6% on ivy.

In competitive interactions won by a honeybee, the honeybee either displaced other flower visitors – for example, by landing on them or pushing them off flowers – or chased them away, in about 20% of cases.

Bumblebees were also observed displacing other pollinators, though Buckle believes this was probably not intentional, and was instead a reflection of their less coordinated movements as they fly through confined spaces.

“They bumble along the patch and then they’ll mistakenly bump into another pollinator and it just falls off a flower,” Buckle said. “With the honeybees, the aggression was more overt. You could tell that they’re specifically trying to move the other one off the flower.”

The reasons for honeybees’ aggressive behaviour is likely to relate to the way in which they organise their social groups, said Buckle, adding: “Some castes of bees can be guard bees, so they have that capacity within them to show threat and aggression, to guard their hives and to look after the brood.”

The only pollinator able to hold its own against honeybees was the ivy bee, which was first recorded in the UK in 2001 and feeds mainly on the nectar of ivy flowers. It was seen displacing and chasing honeybees.

The study also found that higher temperatures led to an increased number of competitive interactions, probably because nectar was drying up and plants were going into heat stress. Given that mean summer temperatures are predicted to rise by up to 4C in the UK by 2080, such competition is likely to become more frequent, said Buckle.

More research is needed to examine how wild pollinators can be better protected, she added.

“A lot of beekeepers are environmentally minded and they want to make sure that they’re not impinging or having an impact on other pollinators,” Buckle said. “This research is important because it helps guide our planning and best practices for conservation.”

title: Stinky business: south London bike shop hit by ‘unbearable’ stench from Thames Water sewer
excerpt:
Owner and mechanics fear for their health and future of the Herne Hill shop with no date for fixing problem

The leafy south London neighbourhood of Herne Hill is a haven for cyclists who can often be...
body_text:
Owner and mechanics fear for their health and future of the Herne Hill shop with no date for fixing problem

The leafy south London neighbourhood of Herne Hill is a haven for cyclists who can often be seen lapping the local parks and refuelling at the many cafes that line the suburban streets. But there is something foul in the air of this corner of the capital – and for once it’s not the traffic fumes hitting bicycle riders.

A toxic stench thought to be caused by untreated sewage stuck in Thames Water drains has been emanating from the subterranean depths for months, most likely caused by the summer’s lack of rain.

The stink is so acrid that the Bicycle Nation shop has had to bar some customers and its mechanics have been forced to work on the pavement outside.

The owner of the shop, Tamas Polocz, has repeatedly complained to Thames Water since the smell first hit the shop in June and caused his colleague Nick to vomit.

Last week the troubled water company told Polocz it accepted that a mains sewer directly beneath the shop was to blame, but it has yet to offer him and his team of 11 any date for resolving the problem.

Polocz and his colleagues have been left fearing for their physical and mental health after repeated exposure to the gassy stench. And the outlook for the business is bleak.

The odour comes in putrid wafts that occur at least five times a day, according to a “smell chart” used to log the time and duration of each incident with a description. The words used include “cabbage”, “teargas”, “onions”, “spicy BBQ” and repeated references to “shit”.

When the Guardian first arrived at the shop there was a whiff of rotten eggs but not enough to stop mechanics working inside and customers milling about. But within minutes we were overpowered by a repulsive gas that hit the back of the throat and left us scurrying outside, gagging for air.

“It’s unbearable,” said Polocz. “You can’t be in the shop when it comes.”

He added: “It has a really strong physical presence. This is a smell you take home with you. It’s in your hair, on your skin, sometimes it feels it’s inside your skin. When you go home and cough, you taste it again.”

The ordeal comes after record-breaking temperatures and drought prompted calls for a radical overhaul of an outdated sewage system, just as the Great Stink ushered in new sanitation in the Victorian era.

Thames Water initially suggested the Herne Hill smell was due to a gas leak. But extensive tests by the local gas supplier ruled that out.

Polocz said he had been battling the company every week. “Thames Water have always tried to push me away, or blame others. When they finally accepted liability last week I just broke down. But we still don’t have a date for fixing it.”

The exact cause of the stench remains unknown, but a Thames Water engineer told Polocz it was likely to be linked to the lack of rain. The engineer also told him that a cast-iron ventilation pipe that had previously drawn odours away from the shop had not been replaced.

Experts warn that during dry periods, untreated sewage builds up in pipes with no rainwater to flush it out. Microbial activity in the sewage causes foul-smelling gas to be emitted in wafts, in a similar process to the one that causes flatulence in human digestion.

Prof Barbara Evans, the chair of public health engineering at Leeds University, said: “It sounds like methane and it’s probably unsafe working conditions. Biological processes are cyclical just like in your digestive system, which is why sewer smells come in wafts.”

When Polocz woke up to rainfall, he was hopeful it would flush away the stench. “I looked out through the window at home and thought, oh good, but it didn’t make any difference. Even after the rain there was still the smell. Maybe the rain will eventually clear it, but we don’t know. Something is happening down there that is pushing the smell up.”

Evans said: “The first flushes of rain will probably make things smell worse because it just stirs things up. It needs a lot of rain to clear. There might be some blockage there but it’s impossible to know without a proper inspection.”

Harriet Talbot, a board member of Bicycle Nation, said: “You can’t run a business relying on the weather.” She helped set up a webpage asking for customers to sign up for a collect and repair service to help the shop survive.

Polocz said the shop was currently unsustainable because staff had to evacuate so frequently. “We have to do half a day in the shop and half outside on the pavement. But now the cold weather is coming, we can’t keep doing that.”

And the stress from the stink is taking its toll. Polocz said: “I’m 49, but today I feel 62-ish. We have guys calling in sick. It affects you both physically and mentally.”

Polocz said he laid in bed at night worrying how he would be able to keep the shop going. “The last thought of the day and the first thought of the day are now both the same,” he said. “And I wake up at night thinking: what are we going to do about it? I try to listen to a podcast, but I still keep thinking about the smell. Somehow I’m going to get through this and change back to normal.”

Polocz’s plight is likely to add to calls for an overhaul of London’s Victorian sewage system. Evans said: “This underlines the need for a rethink of our sewers. The system was designed for a climate that we just don’t currently have any more.”

The Guardian asked Thames Water when the problem would be fixed, why it had taken so long to resolve, and whether the company would apologise to Polocz.

A spokesperson replied: “Our teams are investigating the source of an odour reported at a bike shop. Initial investigations have confirmed there are no blockages in the sewers surrounding the property. Odour monitors are to be installed, which will enable engineers to detect, measure and track odorous gases in real time and help determine the exact cause.”

title: Squash down: smaller pumpkins expected this Halloween after drought in England
excerpt:
Data shows 2026 could be worst harvest on record, as growers suggest painting faces on vegetables instead of carving

In the lead-up to Halloween, front porches across the country feature fat, proudly...
body_text:
Data shows 2026 could be worst harvest on record, as growers suggest painting faces on vegetables instead of carving

In the lead-up to Halloween, front porches across the country feature fat, proudly carved pumpkins, lit from within by tea lights.

But this year there is likely to be a shortage due to drought, experts have warned, with the squashes much smaller than usual.

Mini pumpkins will have to be used, and some have suggested that those celebrating the spooky festival draw faces on vegetables instead of carving them.

England has faced a punishing drought for most of this year, which has dramatically affected harvests. Data has found that this year could be the worst harvest on record as farmers struggled to irrigate their crops.

Pumpkins are 90% water, and need a lot of it to grow. The vegetables are native to the Americas and were brought over in the Tudor period, during the 16th century.

Guy Singh-Watson, the founder of organic veg box company Riverford, said: “After such an extraordinarily hot, dry summer, it’s not surprising that Halloween pumpkins are smaller than usual as they are mostly water. But perhaps it’s time we questioned our obsession with giant carving pumpkins in the first place.”

Shunning pumpkins would go some way to bringing the carving of vegetables tradition back to its roots. The custom began in 17th-century Britain while marking the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain, which was when spirits were thought to roam the Earth.

Rather than pumpkins, root vegetables such as celeriac, turnips and mangelwurzels were carved into grotesque faces, and some believed they could ward off evil spirits.

Guy Barter, the chief horticulturalist at the Royal Horticultural Society, said: “Pumpkins are on the small side this year unless heavily watered. Such drought makes watering sufficiently very difficult to accomplish in practice. Pumpkins are relatively drought-tolerant but this year the weather stretched their tolerance to the limit.

“The heat later and some drought stress caused fruits to ripen earlier than usual. Their dry matter content and rind hardness are both excellent so the crop should store well, although commercial pumpkins become worthless the day after Halloween. That’s a pity as they make lovely soups until the new year when the much tastier winter squashes take over.”

Singh-Watson said the growing of a large, watery squash simply to throw it away after Halloween was wasteful, adding: “I’ve enjoyed growing pumpkins before, they’re a lovely crop, but the idea of growing something that’s going to be thrown away has become increasingly difficult to justify. Growing any crop comes with an environmental cost, and generating a mountain of waste without feeding anyone makes little sense.”

The vegetable entrepreneur has been growing a selection of small, colourful squashes and is now selling a box containing a selection including crown prince, red onion, sweet lightning, futsu and stripetti. He said: “This time of the year should be a celebration of the wonderful abundance of seasonal vegetables that see us through autumn and winter. Squash come in an extraordinary variety of shapes, sizes and colours, and offer just as much decorative potential, with considerably more flavour. Let’s paint a face on a squash instead … and then eat it.”

Some gardeners have been trying novel methods to try to get the size of pumpkins up.

Ali Goding, the garden manager at RHS Harlow Carr in North Yorkshire, said: “Pumpkins struggle to grow in heavy clay soil during drought conditions, so the team at RHS garden Harlow Carr have trialled a new, novel way to grow pumpkins this year – in a compost cake which helps retain moisture, humidity and warmth and the results have been fantastic while also benefiting wildlife.

“They have set with hard skins in the heat so should store well and they will also have a good flavour with all that sun.

“Normally we are a bit cool, damp and too far north for them to develop a full flavour – so the extra heat worked out well for us. A good year!”

title: Murder in Malaysia: Justice for Altantuya Shaariibuu
excerpt:
101 East investigates if power and politics are protecting those behind the 2006 murder of Mongolian woman in Malaysia.

Twenty years ago, two Malaysian special forces policemen brutally murdered Mong...
body_text:
101 East investigates if power and politics are protecting those behind the 2006 murder of Mongolian woman in Malaysia.

Twenty years ago, two Malaysian special forces policemen brutally murdered Mongolian woman Altantuya Shaariibuu, obliterating her body with C4 military explosives.

But the truth behind why they killed her has yet to be determined, leading to suspicions of a political conspiracy to silence her.

101 East travels to Mongolia, Malaysia, France and Australia to investigate allegations of interference in the criminal trial, Altantuya’s suspected links to an allegedly corrupt submarine deal and claims by the policemen that they acted on the orders of convicted former Prime Minister Najib Razak, who vehemently denies any involvement in the murder.

title: Dem congressional candidate's police record reveals suspensions over stolen gun, insubordination
excerpt: Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, criticizes Senate candidate James Talarico's voting record and campaign absence. Roy claims Talarico's progressive stances on borders and social issues make him deeply out of s...
body_text:
Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, criticizes Senate candidate James Talarico's voting record and campaign absence. Roy claims Talarico's progressive stances on borders and social issues make him deeply out of step with Texas voters.

Johnny Garcia, a candidate for Congress in Texas’ newly redrawn 35th District, faced a pair of suspensions for "job performance," "insubordination" and "conduct or action that would seriously impair job effectiveness" during his time with the Bexar County Sheriff’s Office, records show.

In the first suspension in 2009, Garcia brought a cellular device into a secure area against repeated instruction. The second, in 2020, arose when Garcia left a firearm in an unsecured location, where it was later stolen.

In both cases, Garcia was suspended without pay.

The suspensions, discovered through a public records request, put new scrutiny on a law enforcement career that Garcia has made a central part of his campaign as he wages a race against Republican candidate Carlos De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran. The race, set to fill the seat being vacated by Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, is expected to be significantly more competitive in the upcoming midterms than in years past.

FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON

Johnny Garcia, a candidate for Texas U.S. House District 35, speaks in a forum held by the League of Women Voters of the San Antonio Area in the Sidney Board Room at Brooks in San Antonio on Wednesday, May 6, 2026 (Katina Zentz/San Antonio Express-News via Getty Images)

The first suspension came in 2009 when Garcia carried his cell phone into a secured jail area, something he had been told repeatedly not to do.

"You have been instructed multiple times not to bring cellular phones or electronic equipment into the secured area and that doing so is a violation of policy. You stated you had been informed several times during Roll Call that cellular phones are not permitted in the secured area," a notice of suspension reads.

"You are hereby notified that the Bexar County Sheriff’s Department is suspending you without pay for a total of three days… for insubordination [and] conduct or action that would seriously impair job effectiveness."

The second suspension, according to the disciplinary record, came in 2020 when Garcia left his Glock firearm, four magazines and his badge in his car — items that were later stolen.

"Your equipment was not properly secured and was kept temporarily in your vehicle against Bexar County Sheriff’s policy. This negligent behavior has seriously impaired your job effectiveness and is a clear violation of the policies and procedures of the Bexar County Sheriff’s Office," a report read.

Garcia received a five-day suspension without pay, for "job performance," according to the county's records. The firearm was eventually recovered after Garcia reported it was missing.

The Sheriff’s Office did not address questions about additional context on the suspensions, how frequently such suspensions are imposed and what other kinds of discipline the office would consider ahead of a suspension. Instead, it confirmed that Garcia had not faced any other forms of discipline as a result of the two incidents.

TRUMP-BACKED AIR FORCE VETERAN WINS GOP RUNOFF IN NEWLY-REDISTRICTED HOUSE DISTRICT

The Bexar County Sheriff's Office. (Google Maps)

"The Bexar County Sheriff’s Office handles all policy violations in strict accordance with Civil Service Commission guidelines. Deputy Johnny Garcia served a 3-day unpaid suspension for bringing an electronic device into a secure facility, and a 5-day unpaid suspension for failing to properly secure county issued equipment. The disciplinary actions were the agency's final decision of the incidents," Deputy Noel Diaz said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"All deputies are required to maintain complete knowledge of the Civil Service Commission policies. Disciplinary actions are handled independently on single incidents," she added.

Garcia, who has not held elected office before, faces considerably steeper election odds than other Democrats who have run in Texas’ 35th District.

Casar, a progressive, last won re-election in the old district through a 67.4% to 32.6% victory in 2024. But Republicans targeted that electoral advantage through redistricting changes passed last year, prompting Casar to seek re-election in the state’s neighboring 37th district.

"Trump and Abbott just rammed through maps designed to kick people like me out of office. They don’t want me in Congress because they don’t want us to be heard. But we’re not going anywhere," Casar said in a post explaining his move.

To overcome that shift in political advantage, Garcia has brought a centrist message to voters, highlighting his service with the Bexar County Sheriff’s Office, a post he joined at the age of 21. He would go on to work with the county jail and then as a hostage negotiator.

On his website, Garcia lists border security as a top priority alongside items like affordability and protecting government programs like Social Security. He said he had faced border weakness firsthand, stating that he had seen "how Biden failed us on the border."

"An old school Democrat … he believes true public safety means more than tough talk," his website states.

SUPREME COURT HANDS GOP A REDISTRICTING WIN BY STRIKING DOWN LOWER COURT BLOCK ON TEXAS MAP

UNITED STATES - JULY 16: Congressional Progressive Caucus chairman Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, speaks during the news conference on the new Congressional Progressive Caucus task forces ahead of the 2026 election in the U.S. Capitol on Wednesda, July 16, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images) (Fox News)

When asked about the two suspensions, Garcia’s campaign pointed back at his record with safety as a law enforcement officer.

"As a sheriff's deputy, I've spent nearly two decades putting my own safety on the line to protect my community to keep violent criminals off our streets. These politicized claims are Republicans' desperate attempts to distract from the fact that tariffs and his war in Iran have made everything more expensive for working families," Garcia said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Having cleared his party's primary in in May, Garcia heads to the state's general election on Nov. 3.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Rubio’s Uzbekistan trip underlines Central Asia’s hunt for diverse partners
excerpt:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is arriving in Samarkand, the fabled Silk Road city in what is now central Uzbekistan, for talks with key regional ministers on Saturday.

The C5+1 – Centr...
body_text:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is arriving in Samarkand, the fabled Silk Road city in what is now central Uzbekistan, for talks with key regional ministers on Saturday.

The C5+1 – Central Asia plus the US – summit to be held from Saturday to Tuesday heralds Washington’s new approach to the ex-Soviet region – pragmatic, purely transactional and devoid of speeches about democratisation and human rights.

At the dawn of Central Asia’s independence, Americans used to show up in the mostly Muslim region strategically stretched between Russia, China and Iran, bearing gifts – and giving lectures.

After the 1991 Soviet collapse, amid the region’s economic degradation, joblessness and poverty, US and European diplomats and businessmen were seen as ambassadors of the brave new world of capitalist prosperity.

They wanted reforms – and not just the economic ones.

Western diplomats made sure that former Communist apparatchiks-turned-new regional leaders understood that they’d get investments, technologies and international recognition only in exchange for abandoning the Soviet-era totalitarian ways of governing and building the economy.

The West held forums and workshops on human rights, democracy and decentralisation of governance, and sent thousands of students and officials to Western schools.

And the West accused regional leaders of losing their moral compass and threatened sanctions when they began to amend their nation’s constitutions to extend their presidential terms, appoint their family members and friends to key government jobs and help them create business empires that often competed with Western investors.

“When the West began moralising, teaching them about democracy, human rights, they immediately turned towards China or Russia,” Galiya Ibragimova, Uzbekistan-born, Moldova-based regional expert, told Al Jazeera.

Uzbekistan, the region’s most populous nation of 37 million, offers a perfect example.

Its iron-fisted President Islam Karimov was the first ex-Soviet leader to allow a US military base on its soil in 2001.

But four years later, he kicked it out after Washington lambasted his brutal suppression of a popular revolt in the eastern city of Andijan that killed hundreds of unarmed civilians.

In 2005, a leaked US diplomatic cable called Karimov’s daughter, Gulnara, a “robber baron” who forcibly took over lucrative businesses and was seen as her father’s successor.

As to moralising and lecturing, the tables have turned since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, observers say.

Moscow still has plenty of soft power in Central Asia – from movies and pop music to theatre festivals and propagandist TV shows that constantly lie about the war.

The Kremlin also uses its economic clout to promote the imperialist concept of the “Russian World”, where the region is seen as Moscow’s “near abroad”, and its pre-Russian heritage is snubbed as backwards and insignificant.

In 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed that Kazakhstan had “never had statehood”, and his ideological allies repeatedly threatened to annex its Russian-speaking northern part.

This year, Kazakhstan began extraditing Kremlin critics and supplying gas to Russia amid Ukrainian drone attacks on its oil refineries.

In January, Kremlin propagandist Vladimir Solovyov said Moscow should launch a “special military operation” – a term reserved for the war in Ukraine – in Central Asia and Armenia.

Critical remarks from minor political figures followed – but no rebukes from the halls of real power.

Meanwhile, Central Asian labour migrants have been duped or forced into enlisting to fight in Ukraine in droves, while Moscow uses Central Asian companies to import microchips, communications equipment and machine tools to build drones and missiles.

“These days, the US and Russia have switched roles. Today, it’s Russia that began building ties through moralising,” Ibragimova, the regional expert, said.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump’s administration has abandoned the pro-democracy stance and now advocates a utilitarian, transactional approach to foreign policy.

“Under Trump, the American policy in Central Asia is all about ‘just business and nothing more’, without being nosy about human rights, reforms. They are content with everything,” Ibragimova said.

Earlier this month, Trump received Saida Mirziyoyeva, the daughter of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.

A year earlier, Mirziyoyev pledged to invest up to $100bn in the US economy, buy Boeing aircraft and even US-grown cotton, even though Uzbekistan is one of the world’s largest cotton growers.

Washington did not say a word about Mirziyoyev’s crackdown on critics or his daughter’s growing domestic clout.

After largely ignoring Central Asia during Trump’s first term, the White House wants to resume its presence.

“The interest is mostly geopolitical and military-strategic, considering the region’s location in the zone of Russia’s and China’s interests,” Alisher Ilkhamov, head of the London-based Central Asia Due Diligence think tank, told Al Jazeera.

“In the future, Washington apparently wants to have a military base here as a deterrent measure against China,” he said.

The economic interests seem to be focused on rare-earth minerals – crucial for manufacturing a wide array of technology – and other critical elements, especially since China uses them as a political cudgel in its ties with Washington.

The deposits are abundant, but need development, technologies and investment.

Meanwhile, the White House shows little interest in human rights violations in Central Asia, such as the jailing of political opponents and independent journalists.

“An interest in these issues, unfortunately, is absent from Rubio’s agenda, because these problems went missing from US foreign policy priorities since Trump returned to the White House,” Ilkhamov said.

A Norwegian human rights advocate echoes his concerns.

“There are uncomfortable similarities between Trump’s worldview and established authoritarian regimes like Tajikistan and Turkmenistan,” Ivar Dale, a senior policy adviser with the Norwegian Helsinki Committee, a rights watchdog, told Al Jazeera.

“However, Marco Rubio probably has a better understanding of Central Asia and the challenges there than does [Vice President] JD Vance and [Defense Secretary] Pete Hegseth,” he said.

The US State Department “should bring back the focus [on human rights] if the C5+1 format is to be taken seriously going forward”, he said.
