title: Bryan Kohberger fights to remove judge who called him 'worst of the worst,' questioned his honesty
excerpt: Idaho prosecutors urge a judge to reject murder suspect Bryan Kohberger's attempt to withdraw his guilty plea, calling the defense's arguments a fishing expedition. Former federal prosecutor Jonathan ...
body_text:
Idaho prosecutors urge a judge to reject murder suspect Bryan Kohberger's attempt to withdraw his guilty plea, calling the defense's arguments a fishing expedition. Former federal prosecutor Jonathan Fahey joins to break down the latest legal maneuvers, the strength of the state's case and what lies ahead for the victims' families in the high-profile trial.

Bryan Kohberger's new lawyer is taking another swing at Idaho prosecutors in his fight to have the judge who called his client a "faceless coward" removed from post-conviction proceedings.

Court-appointed attorney Greg Rauch is accusing Latah County prosecutors of "regurgitating" rules rather than addressing concerns raised in his motion to disqualify Judge Steven Hippler from the case.

Hippler said Kohberger, 31, "slithered" into the victims' home before committing a crime that made him "the worst of the worst" after the killer admitted guilt last year.

At issue, according to Rauch, "is how [Hippler's] statements about counsel’s preparation and [Kohberger's] capacity for truthfulness bear on the disputes it may now decide, in combination with the myriad of other statements made."

KOHBERGER PROSECUTORS SAY NO AS IDAHO KILLER TRIES TO BOOT JUDGE WHO CALLED HIM A 'FACELESS COWARD'

Judge Steven Hippler of Idaho's 4th Judicial District in Ada County rejected the latest attempt by Bryan Kohberger's defense to drop the death penalty as a possible sentence if a jury convicts him of killing four University of Idaho students in 2022. (Katherine Jones/Idaho Statesman/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

And when addressing the fact that there would be no allocution or explanation from Kohberger, the judge also questioned whether Kohberger even possessed the capacity to say something truthful.

"Even if I could force him to speak, which legally I cannot, how could anyone ever be assured that what he speaks is the truth?" Hippler asked during sentencing. "Do we really believe, after all of this, he is capable of speaking the truth, or of giving up something of himself to help the very people whose lives he destroyed? Rather, I suspect the so-called reason would be dished out in enticing self-serving and aggrandizing untruthful bits, leaving people wanting more information, more insight, and thus enhancing even further the power he seeks to hold."

BRYAN KOHBERGER DIDN'T UNDERSTAND WHAT HE WAS DOING WHEN HE PLEADED GUILTY: UNSEALED MEMO

Bryan Kohberger appeared at the Ada County Courthouse for his sentencing hearing on July 23, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. Kohberger pleaded guilty in exchange for being spared the death penalty for the stabbing of four University of Idaho students nearly three years earlier. (Kyle Green-Pool/Getty Images)

Rauch wrote that "of course" judges can deny defense motions, "condemn terrible crimes," and go on to preside over post-conviction claims.

BRYAN KOHBERGER'S NEW LAWYER SAYS KEY QUESTIONS MAY SOON GET ANSWERS IN COURT

"The question is not whether someone might criticize the Court, but whether an informed, reasonable observer could question its impartiality in light of this connected record," he wrote.

And it's not just that Hippler tore into Kohberger at sentencing. He has also taken issue with a June scheduling order days before Kohberger surprised the country and pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty.

University of Idaho students Madison Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin were killed in a November 2022 attack at an off-campus house on King Road in Moscow, Idaho. (Idaho Statesman/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

"This motion does not rest upon one adverse ruling, one harsh statement, or the mere fact that the judge who presided over Bryan Kohberger’s criminal case has been assigned to his post-conviction proceeding," Rauch wrote in his initial 22-page motion on Aug. 27. "It rests upon the extraordinary convergence of all of them."

Hippler had rejected a request for more time for Kohberger's previous defense lawyer, Anne Taylor, and in a June 26 order, described her complaints about discovery as "ultimately empty" while suggesting she was simply trying to delay his trial.

IDAHO PROSECUTORS ACCUSE BRYAN KOHBERGER OF 'FISHING' TO FIND BETTER ARGUMENTS FOR BID TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA

Six days later, at a change-of-plea hearing, Hippler asked Taylor, "Have you been able to do all the discovery you feel necessary?"

Bryan Kohberger's lawyer, Gregory Rauch in Boise, Idaho. (Derek Shook for Fox News Digital)

BRYAN KOHBERGER WAIVED HIS APPEAL RIGHTS BUT PLANS ON PURSUING POST-CONVICTION RELIEF

Prosecutors, in an opposition to the motion filed earlier this month, wrote that Kohberger had failed to show Hippler "is biased."

Outgoing Latah County Prosecuting Attorney Bill Thompson, who announced his retirement earlier this week, and Deputy Prosecuting Attorney Keith Scholl wrote that Hippler's statements about Kohberger after he'd admitted to killing four innocent students were not unusual or out of line.

BRYAN KOHBERGER’S 2027 HEARING IS NOT GUARANTEED AS IDAHO SEEKS QUICK DISMISSAL

Latah County Prosecutor, Bill Thompson walks across the carpark at Latah County Courthouse, Moscow, Idaho, Friday, August 7, 2026. (Derek Shook for Fox News Digital)

"In our case, the sentencing remarks are not enough to show bias, and the required showing of perceived bias cannot be tied to this Court's capacity to fairly adjudicate any [post-conviction relief] claims alleged in this case but rather puts this Court in the best position to adjudicate them as the legislature and the Idaho Supreme Court's rules intend," they wrote.

BRYAN KOHBERGER'S POST-CONVICTION RELIEF BID ENABLED BY FLAWED PLEA DEAL, PSYCHOLOGIST ARGUES

Rauch also argued that Hippler could voluntarily recuse himself from the case to avoid any appearance of partiality.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

In the new 12-page filing, Rauch also argued that prosecutors have attributed concessions to his client that were never made, mischaracterized his initial motion and failed to address some of the arguments he did make in it.

Bryan Kohberger appeared at the Ada County Courthouse, Wednesday, July 2, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. (AP Photo/Kyle Green, Pool)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

"The State’s Response does not resolve this motion by repeating the ordinary rule, supplying concessions Petitioner never made, or calling the disputed statements routine," Rauch wrote.

Kohberger is attempting to undo his guilty plea in the University of Idaho student murders that killed Madison Mogen, 21, Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, 20, in November 2022.

The former criminology Ph.D. student initially filed a handwritten petition for post-conviction relief in July.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Rauch was later appointed to represent him and has until Jan. 13, 2027 to file an amended petition that is expected to be much more in-depth than Kohberger's.

Bryan Kohberger arrived at Monroe County Courthouse in Pennsylvania in advance of an extradition hearing. (The Image Direct for Fox News Digital)

"A request for an impartial adjudicator is certainly not a request for a sympathetic one," he wrote. "Reassignment would change the judge, not the evidence or the governing law."

A hearing on the matter was supposed to take place Thursday, before Hippler abruptly canceled it and said it would be rescheduled later.

title: Internet owes Panthers forward Brady Tkachuk big apology after second consecutive hat trick
excerpt: NHL players and Olympic gold medalists Brady and Matthew Tkachuk discuss the pride of representing the USA in sports. They reflect on their Olympic hockey wins and offer advice to the current US socce...
body_text:
NHL players and Olympic gold medalists Brady and Matthew Tkachuk discuss the pride of representing the USA in sports. They reflect on their Olympic hockey wins and offer advice to the current US soccer team in the World Cup.

When the Florida Panthers acquired forward Brady Tkachuk in a trade with the Ottawa Senators over the summer, hockey fans and pundits everywhere bemoaned the fact that an already established champion was slowly becoming a super team.

And who could blame them? After all, the Cats were coming off of winning back-to-back Stanley Cups just 12 months earlier, and the only reason they missed the playoffs in 2026 was due in large part to a historic rash of injuries to some of their biggest stars.

Adding Tkachuk seemed like a case of the rich getting richer, as Florida recovered to full strength while adding one of the best young players in the game to their roster.

Matthew Tkachuk and Brady Tkachuk of the Florida Panthers skate during the third period against the Carolina Hurricanes at Lenovo Center in Raleigh, N.C., on Sept. 29, 2026. (Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images)

For the first couple weeks of the season, it looked like the addition of Matthew's younger brother was all smoke and mirrors, with Brady being held to zero points through the first five games of the year.

Rival fans were quick to jump all over this fact, given that both the Panthers and the Tkachuk brothers were seen as polarizing villains throughout the NHL.

The internet had a field day, but just as the fans started to take their victory laps, Brady got hot.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

After breaking the points seal three games prior with an assist in a 5-3 loss in Buffalo, the younger Tkachuk brother notched back-to-back hat tricks in wins over Columbus on Tuesday and Vancouver on Thursday, becoming the first to do so since fellow American Auston Matthews in 2024.

His three goals against the Canucks proved to be the difference, too, as the Cats needed every bit of Brady's offensive prowess to squeak out a 3-2 victory in overtime.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Brady Tkachuk is congratulated by his brother Matthew Tkachuk after scoring a goal during the second period against the Columbus Blue Jackets at Nationwide Arena in Columbus, Ohio, on Oct. 13, 2026. (NHLI via Getty Images)

Matthew became the first player in NHL history to assist his brother on all three goals of a natural hat trick.

In short, the Tkachuk brothers are on fire, and if they can carry the water for Florida - along with other Panthers like Sam Bennett, Sam Reinhart, and Seth Jones - while Brad Marchand and captain Aleksander Barkov are out with injuries, the Cats could be a dangerous team heading into the new year.

Florida Panthers' Aleksander Barkov, right, celebrates his goal with Florida Panthers' Matthew Tkachuk (19) as Carolina Hurricanes goaltender Pyotr Kochetkov (52) looks on during the third period of Game 2 of the NHL hockey Stanley Cup Eastern Conference finals in Raleigh, N.C., Thursday, May 22, 2025. (AP Photo/Karl DeBlaker)

There's still almost a full season of hockey to play, but there are plenty of Eastern Conference teams who will be looking under their beds at night now that Florida seems to have their mojo back.

title: Major US grocery chains hit by cybersecurity incident
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You pull out your phone to check your grocery store's digital coupons or place an order for dinner. Suddenly, the app ...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You pull out your phone to check your grocery store's digital coupons or place an order for dinner. Suddenly, the app won't open. The website is unavailable, and the groceries you were counting on for tonight may never arrive. For anyone who depends on online grocery shopping, that's a frustrating problem.

That's the situation shoppers encountered this week at several major U.S. supermarket chains. A cybersecurity incident at grocery giant Ahold Delhaize forced the company to take some systems offline. The disruption affected Stop & Shop, Food Lion, Hannaford and the Giant supermarket chains. The company says its physical stores have remained open, although customers have experienced interruptions to online services.

There's another reason this story deserves attention. The same company suffered a major data breach in 2024 that exposed personal information belonging to more than 2.2 million people. So, as investigators work to understand the latest incident, shoppers have a reasonable question: Could their personal information be at risk again?

CHICK-FIL-A DATA BREACH EXPOSES CUSTOMER ACCOUNTS

Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com.

FRENCH SUPERMARKETS FACE MILLIONS IN LOSSES AFTER CYBERATTACK HITS REFRIGERATORS NATIONWIDE

Stop & Shop is among five major U.S. supermarket chains that experienced online service disruptions following a cybersecurity incident at parent company Ahold Delhaize. (Ahold Delhaize)

On Oct. 12, Ahold Delhaize confirmed a cybersecurity issue within its network. The Netherlands-based company owns some of America's best-known regional supermarket chains and operates more than 9,400 stores worldwide. The company took certain systems offline to protect its operations while security teams investigated the problem. In its official statement, Ahold Delhaize said: "Our teams are taking steps to assess and mitigate the issue. This includes taking some systems offline to help protect them."

The company serves approximately 60 million customers each week across its international businesses. Consequently, a problem involving its technology can affect grocery shopping far beyond a single store.

The cybersecurity incident has disrupted online services for five major U.S. supermarket chains:

According to Grocery Dive, websites and mobile apps for all five chains were still unavailable on the morning of Wednesday, Oct. 14. That marked at least the third consecutive day of online disruptions. Customers have encountered problems accessing online ordering and digital coupons. Some app-based loyalty features have also been unavailable. In its Oct. 13 update, Ahold Delhaize said it was beginning a controlled relaunch of certain systems. However, as of Oct. 14, the company had not announced a firm timetable for restoring all affected services.

Yes. In its Oct. 13 statement, Ahold Delhaize confirmed that its supermarkets across Europe and the United States remained open and were serving customers. Notices from the affected U.S. chains also indicated that pharmacies were operating during their normal business hours. However, online shopping has experienced significant disruptions. Customers have faced interruptions to grocery pickup and delivery services. Meanwhile, shoppers who rely on digital coupons have encountered problems accessing their usual discounts.

As of Oct. 14, Food Lion, Giant Food and The Giant Company also directed customers to third-party delivery services, including Instacart, DoorDash and Uber Eats, where available. For customers who depend on grocery delivery because of mobility challenges or limited transportation, these disruptions can create a serious inconvenience.

Food Lion stores remain open despite cybersecurity-related disruptions affecting the supermarket chain's website, mobile app and online ordering services. (Food Lion)

If you placed an online grocery order that was never fulfilled, the affected supermarket chains said customers would receive refunds for those orders. However, it's worth checking your credit card or bank account to make sure the refund actually arrives.

Keep your original order confirmation and any emails related to the purchase. If the refund doesn't appear within the retailer's stated processing period, contact customer service through a verified channel. If your grocery app remains unavailable, shopping inside a physical store may be your most dependable option. Still, consider calling ahead if you need a specific service or want to confirm that a prescription is ready.

On Oct. 13, Ahold Delhaize issued a statement, updated Oct. 14, saying it was in the process of starting a controlled relaunch of certain systems. The company said it was working with external cybersecurity experts and appropriate authorities to investigate the incident. In a direct response to CyberGuy, an Ahold Delhaize USA spokesperson provided an update on efforts to restore affected services. "Please know our teams are working as quickly as possible to restore systems safely that we took offline as a precautionary measure, including our websites," the spokesperson told CyberGuy.

The spokesperson also confirmed that stores remain open and apologized for the disruption to customers. However, Ahold Delhaize has not publicly identified who caused the problem or explained how its network was compromised. It has also not confirmed whether ransomware played a role. That leaves several important questions unanswered, including how the incident began and when all affected services will be restored. The company has not provided a firm timetable for full restoration.

This may be the biggest concern for shoppers who have online grocery accounts. In its statement, Ahold Delhaize said investigators had found no evidence at that point that customer, employee or partner data was taken during the incident. That's encouraging for shoppers who have provided personal information to these supermarket chains. However, investigators were still examining the incident as of that update. The company's preliminary findings do not definitively rule out data theft. As of Oct. 14, Ahold Delhaize had not confirmed that personal information was stolen during this latest incident. That means shoppers should remain alert without assuming their personal information has been compromised.

Unfortunately, this isn't the first major cybersecurity incident involving Ahold Delhaize. In November 2024, hackers gained unauthorized access to internal U.S. business systems operated by Ahold Delhaize USA Services. The attackers obtained files containing sensitive personal information. The company eventually disclosed that more than 2.2 million people were affected. According to a filing with the Maine Attorney General, the breach involved approximately 2.24 million individuals. In a June 2025 breach notification, the company explained that the stolen information varied by person.

The vast majority of those affected were current or former employees, along with their dependents and beneficiaries. The company said it had no indication that customer payment or pharmacy systems were compromised during the 2024 attack. The ransomware group INC Ransom claimed responsibility for the earlier incident. However, Ahold Delhaize did not publicly confirm the group's involvement. There is currently no confirmed connection between that attack and the October 2026 cybersecurity incident.

For many of us, grocery shopping now involves much more than walking into a store with a shopping list. We create accounts, save payment details and use loyalty programs to access discounts. Some families depend on online ordering every week. When a supermarket chain experiences a cybersecurity incident, those conveniences can suddenly disappear. For Ahold Delhaize, the challenge now extends beyond restoring its apps. The company also faces questions about the security of its systems after experiencing two major incidents in less than two years. Customers deserve to understand what happened once investigators have reliable answers.

Grocery shoppers increasingly rely on mobile apps for digital coupons and online orders, making cybersecurity-related outages especially frustrating. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Even without confirmed customer data theft, a widely reported cybersecurity incident can give scammers opportunities to target shoppers. These seven precautions can help you protect your information and avoid additional headaches.

Scammers may send emails or text messages claiming that you need to verify your payment information to receive a grocery refund. Those messages can seem especially convincing if you've recently had an order canceled. Avoid clicking unexpected refund links. Instead, review your original payment account or contact the retailer using a verified phone number. Never provide your banking password or pay a processing fee to receive a refund.

If you placed an order around the time of the outage, check whether the store charged you for groceries you never received. Save your confirmation emails and keep any receipts. Then, review your account for a refund. If the money doesn't appear within the retailer's stated processing period, contact customer service or your payment provider.

If you reuse your grocery account password on other websites, replace it with a unique one. A password manager can generate and store strong passwords without forcing you to remember each one. Also, enable two-factor authentication (2FA) if your grocery account supports it. That gives your account another layer of protection against unauthorized access.

A real cybersecurity incident gives scammers an opportunity to send convincing fake breach notifications. You might receive a message claiming that your grocery account has been compromised and that you must immediately verify your identity. Before entering personal information, confirm the alert through the retailer's official communications.

Although Ahold Delhaize reported no evidence of data theft in its Oct. 14 update, regularly checking your financial accounts remains a smart precaution. Enable transaction alerts through your bank or credit card provider. Pay attention to unfamiliar charges or unexpected account activity.

If you normally use your grocery store's app to access digital coupons or loyalty rewards, check your receipt carefully. Some discounts may be unavailable while the retailer's online services are down. Before checking out, ask a store employee whether there's another way to receive an advertised discount. Keep your receipt if you believe you were overcharged so you can request an adjustment when customer service becomes available.

If you clicked a suspicious grocery refund or security alert link, your next steps depend on what information you shared. If you entered your password, change it immediately through the retailer's official website once it's available. Update any other accounts using that password. If you provided credit card or banking information, contact your financial institution and ask about securing your account. You can also report suspected fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov. If you downloaded a suspicious attachment, run a security scan using strong antivirus software on your device. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

I find it troubling that a company responsible for feeding millions of American families is dealing with another major cybersecurity incident so soon after its last one. We depend on grocery stores for something as basic as putting dinner on the table. Increasingly, those stores also want us to use their apps to access the best prices and place orders. What concerns me is how quickly those everyday conveniences can disappear when something goes wrong with a retailer's technology. And after the 2024 breach exposed personal information belonging to more than 2.2 million people, I think Ahold Delhaize has some serious questions to answer. I'd like to know what caused this latest incident and whether the company addressed weaknesses identified after the previous attack. Those answers could go a long way toward restoring customer confidence. As of the company's October 14 update, investigators had found no evidence that customer, employee or partner data was taken in the latest incident. That's reassuring, although the investigation continues. In the meantime, you should remain cautious about unexpected refund messages or suspicious security alerts.

If your grocery store suffered two major cybersecurity incidents in less than two years, would you still trust it with your personal information, or would you take your business somewhere else? Let us know by writing to us at CybergGuy.com.

title: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia fired after five days on the job
excerpt:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is “transitioning out” of her role just one week after United States President Donald Trump tapped her for the job, Al Jazeera has confirmed.

Fox News on Fr...
body_text:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is “transitioning out” of her role just one week after United States President Donald Trump tapped her for the job, Al Jazeera has confirmed.

Fox News on Friday reported that Trump said there was no rush to hire Zacharia’s replacement.

Earlier Friday, Trump told reporters he told Zacharia to “reconsider” staying in the job.

“I don’t think Katie should be made to suffer like she’s suffering at the hands of the press,” Trump said as he departed the White House. “I said to her, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. You think about it.’”

Zacharia said she had received a call about the role last week. She succeeded Karoline Leavitt.

Trump later announced her appointment and described her as “an attorney”. However, over the last week, the question of whether Zacharia, a graduate of California’s Pepperdine University law school, had actually passed the bar exam to work as an attorney came under fire.

In an interview, she told Fox News on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam.

She lasted five days on the job, half the length of Anthony Scaramucci’s tenure as director of communications, who served for 10 days during Trump’s first administration.

Al Jazeera correspondent Kimberly Halkett explained that the appointment and subsequent reversal could create further problems for Trump as Republicans prepare for a pivotal midterm election.

“The fact that there was that major credibility issue as well as a shaky performance is what sealed her fate,” said Halkett. “This makes the president look impulsive at a time when he’s already being criticised for not having a campaign that is really on track to win in November.”

title: Kenya records third Ebola case, linked to first patient who died
excerpt: Kenya has recorded its third case of the Bundibugyo virus disease – a strain of Ebola that has killed thousands of people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) – 10 days after reporting its fi...
body_text:
Kenya has recorded its third case of the Bundibugyo virus disease – a strain of Ebola that has killed thousands of people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) – 10 days after reporting its first case and death in Nairobi.

The latest confirmed case – a 65-year-old woman – was a “primary contact and a close relative of the first and second cases”, Kenya’s Health Ministry said in a statement on Friday, adding that the patient has been in quarantine since October 6.

After developing symptoms, she was isolated and then tested positive for the virus, it added in a statement.

“Once she developed fever, sore throat and malaise, she was isolated and specimen collected for testing. She tested positive for Ebola,” the Health Ministry said. “She was diagnosed early and is currently receiving ⁠⁠supportive care improving her ⁠⁠chances of recovery.”

Kenya’s cases are linked to the Ebola epidemic in the DRC, which is the second-largest on record globally ⁠ ⁠with more than 9,000 cases and over 4,300 deaths since it was officially detected in May.

Kenya’s ⁠⁠first case emerged last ⁠⁠week after a Kenyan man, who had been ill in the DRC about a month before travelling by road ‌‌to Uganda, flew to Nairobi on October 3, where a relative drove him to ‌‌the ‌‌hospital. He died on October 5.

In its statement on X, the Health Ministry moved to reassure the public that there was no community spread of the disease and that the risk to the Kenyan public remained low.

Out of 130 contacts listed, 127 had been traced and were in quarantine, it said.

Efforts to control the spread of the Ebola outbreak have been complicated because the Bundibugyo strain has no licensed vaccine. Research is under way to develop one or more vaccines that work against the strain and some of these vaccines are already in the early phases of testing in humans.

The new case in Kenya was reported as Africa’s ‌‌top public health body and Congolese health authorities called ⁠⁠for greater transparency in how Ebola response funds are used.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said financial information provided by aid organisations indicated that ⁠⁠more than $700m of donor money was unaccounted for.

Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of ‌‌the Africa CDC, told the Reuters news agency that international donors disbursed about $962m to organisations ⁠⁠implementing Ebola response activities in DRC, rather ⁠⁠than to the government.

Kaseya said those organisations reported receiving $228m, of which $127m had ⁠⁠been spent and roughly $100m remained available.

But he said it was too early to speak of embezzlement.

In a post on X, Congolese Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba warned aid groups were required to provide details on funding ‌‌sources to his ministry or risk being barred from working ‌‌in ‌‌DRC and blacklisted across Africa.

Meanwhile, on the ground in the DRC, Ebola cases have been detected in a new province bordering the Central African Republic, two health officials told Reuters on Thursday.

The two cases were confirmed in North Ubangi, the eighth Congolese province affected by the Bundibugyo outbreak, the officials said. Congolese authorities have not yet officially announced the outbreak has spread to North Ubangi.

title: I lost half my right lung to cancer. Pope Leo's diagnosis gives me hope
excerpt: Pulmonologist Dr. Cedric Rutland joins 'Fox & Friends' to share medical insights on Pope Leo's health following lung cancer surgery. Dr. Rutland explains the typical recovery process for lung surgery,...
body_text:
Pulmonologist Dr. Cedric Rutland joins 'Fox & Friends' to share medical insights on Pope Leo's health following lung cancer surgery. Dr. Rutland explains the typical recovery process for lung surgery, noting why the pope is expected to remain in the hospital for a week.

When Pope Leo told the crowd in St. Peter's Square on Sunday that doctors had found "a small, localized nodule" in his lung, the reassurances came fast. Most nodules are benign, media medical experts quickly said. Probably nothing to worry about.

I heard the same reassurances about my own lung not long ago. They were wrong then, and on Tuesday the Vatican confirmed they were wrong now. The nodule was adenocarcinoma, lung cancer. Surgeons removed the lower lobe of the Holy Father's right lung through a few small incisions, guided by a camera rather than an open chest, and he was back in his room the same afternoon.

POPE LEO DIAGNOSED WITH LUNG CANCER AFTER SURGEONS REMOVE PART OF RIGHT LUNG, VATICAN SAYS

That is almost exactly what happened to me. Half of my right lung was removed just 12 months ago, and I was running just four weeks after that. So, my first reaction when I heard the pope's diagnosis was not dread. It was hope.

I was 43, a mother of four, a daily runner, and the daughter of a lung doctor. The morning I learned I had lung cancer, I had already completed a six-mile run without a hint that anything was wrong. I had no symptoms. Under current guidelines, I was not supposed to be at risk, and I did not qualify for screening.

POPE LEO UNDERGOES BLOOD TESTS, X-RAY FOLLOWING CANCER SURGERY, VATICAN SAYS

My diagnosis came from a scan I chose, not from a symptom. My husband and I have always leaned toward proactive testing, and at his urging I scheduled what I assumed would be a baseline full-body scan, paid for out of pocket. It showed a 3.8-centimeter nodule on my right lung. Initial advice from the reading radiologist recommended to follow-up if symptoms occurred. But with a father as a lung doctor and a friend as a lung radiologist, they pushed me to follow up sooner. The new low dose CT of my chest showed the mass had grown in just two months. But that scan led to a diagnosis of stage 1B lung cancer and, like the pope, to surgery to remove it. Still, no symptoms ever appeared.

Four weeks to the day after my operation, I was on a plane. I was running again within weeks. Caught early and handled by a skilled medical team and a surgeon who does this every day, lung cancer is not a death sentence. It is a survivable disease, a fixable problem. If the pope keeps his November trip to South America, he will board that plane about as far out from surgery as I was.

DR MARC SIEGEL: POPE LEO'S LUNG SURGERY PUTS MODERN MEDICINE ALONGSIDE FAITH

So the gloom I see in my text threads with Catholic friends this week is misplaced. What should worry Americans is something else entirely. The pope's cancer was found during a routine checkup. Mine was found because I paid for a scan no one recommended. Most Americans get neither.

Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States and one of the most expensive cancers to treat, because it is usually found late. Current guidelines recommend screening only for adults ages 50 to 80 with a heavy smoking history. Fewer than one in five people who qualify ever get the scan. And nearly two-thirds of people diagnosed with lung cancer would not have qualified at all. I am one of them.

POPE LEO'S LUNG TUMOR RAISES QUESTIONS ABOUT CANCER RISK FOR NONSMOKERS

Stage at diagnosis is the strongest predictor of both survival and cost. Found at stage I, five-year survival can exceed 90%. Yet most cases are still found after the disease has spread, when curative treatment becomes unlikely.

There is a fix on the table. The Saving Health by Identifying Risk for Americans (SHIRA) Act, a draft bill now circulating in the White House, HHS and Congress, would make lung cancer screening free to the patient under Medicare — no copay, no deductible. It would cover veterans exposed to burn pits, guarantee a first scan to cancer survivors and those with a family history, and require Medicare to modernize who counts as "high risk" so that never-smokers, like me, stop being invisible. It builds a path toward age-based screening after 40, the way we already screen for breast and colorectal cancer.

I was fortunate. A preventive scan, a persistent friend and father, and an early diagnosis gave me a future I might not otherwise have had. The pope was fortunate too: a routine check found his cancer before he felt a thing. Luck should not decide who survives lung cancer. Screening policy should.

I am praying for the pope this week, and I am confident. I would like every American to have the same reason for confidence he does.

Shira Kupperman Boehler is a lung cancer survivor, a mother of four, and author of "One Scan Saved My Life: How One Woman's Story Will Change the Way We Detect Lung Cancer."

title: Americans back Trump's decision against livestreaming Nidal Hasan's firing squad execution
excerpt:
Americans are backing President Donald Trump's announcement that Nidal Hasan's execution will not be publicly livestreamed. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Americans interviewed by Fo...
body_text:
Americans are backing President Donald Trump's announcement that Nidal Hasan's execution will not be publicly livestreamed. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Americans interviewed by Fox News Digital were overwhelmingly pleased with President Donald Trump's decision to call off livestreaming the Fort Hood shooter’s planned firing squad execution after the Pentagon had announced it would be livestreamed for public viewing.

"I'm really glad that he called it off, because I feel like it's not really a deterrent, it's more like a shock effect," Sylvia from Arizona told Fox News Digital. "I don't think we really need that in this country right now."

"The only other countries that really do that are like North Korea," David from Arizona said. "We don't want to be North Korea."

AMERICANS DRAW THE LINE AT LIVESTREAMING ‘SPECTACLE’ OF FORT HOOD SHOOTER'S EXECUTION: ‘IT’S AN ABOMINATION’

President Donald Trump and North Korea's leader Kim Jong-un talk before a meeting in the Demilitarized Zone on June 30, 2019, in Panmunjom, Korea. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)

"I never approved of the idea of it being public in the first place," Nate from Virginia said. "I think it's just ridiculous to make a spectacle out of an execution, especially in 2026 of all time."

War Secretary Pete Hegseth announced earlier this month that Nidal Hasan’s execution, set for Dec. 3, would be publicly available via livestream.

Trump took to Truth Social on Thursday to announce that while livestreaming the execution could serve as a deterrent to terrorism, the execution would not be available for public viewing as he acknowledged that many Americans would rather not witness Hasan's death.

"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

FORT HOOD SURVIVORS PRAISE TRUMP FOR SCRAPPING HASAN EXECUTION LIVESTREAM: ‘WE’RE NOT BARBARIC’

President Donald Trump announced that the execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan would not be livestreamed, reversing an earlier Pentagon announcement that the execution would be livestreamed to the public. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images; Bell County Sheriff's Office via Getty Images)

Despite the execution not being publicly available, Trump confirmed that the family members of the victims who died in the 2009 shooting "deserve to witness JUSTICE" and will be permitted to attend in person.

"Well, maybe he has a conscience now," one person said about Trump’s reversal of the Pentagon’s decision to livestream the execution.

Some Americans who spoke with Fox News Digital argued that Trump’s decision to call off the livestreaming was to save face after criticism of the proposal was circulating, with many arguing that livestreaming the execution would turn it into a spectacle and could easily be exposed to children.

"I think it was trying to save his image," Ivy from Georgia said.

"He doesn't wanna look like a bad person, but at the end of the day, we all know who he really is — a piece of s---," Ivy said.

"I think it was just so clearly an unpopular thing to do that he realized it would probably do more harm to his public image than good," Nate said.

Hasan, an Army psychiatrist at the time of the shooting, killed 13 and injured 32 people when he shouted "Allahu Akbar" and opened fire at a military base in Texas. The mass killer is now 56 years old and uses a wheelchair after he was left partially paralyzed from being shot by police officers during his arrest almost 17 years ago.

TRUMP CLEARS WAY FOR FORT HOOD TERRORIST TO FACE ARMY FIRING SQUAD NEARLY 17 YEARS AFTER MASSACRE

Major Nidal Malik Hasan, the U.S. Army doctor identified by authorities as the mass shooter at the U.S. Army post in Fort Hood, Texas, is seen in this undated handout photo from a PDF file of the U.S. Government Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences downloaded on Nov. 6, 2009. (Reuters/Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences/Handout)

Only one person who spoke with Fox News Digital argued that livestreaming the execution would have been a good idea, even adding that he would have watched the livestream himself.

"Yeah, I would watch," Daniel from Virginia said. "Because I wouldn't want somebody to kill another person, you know what I mean? That person should be held wrong for what he's done."

Hasan was sentenced to death during his 2013 military trial after being found guilty on all 42 counts. His execution is set to be the first U.S. military execution in over six decades.

Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: EU rallies in support of Ukraine amid Trump standoff
excerpt: European Union leaders have urged continued support for Ukraine amid a deepening rift between Washington and Kyiv that has raised fears the country could be left more exposed to Russian attacks headin...
body_text:
European Union leaders have urged continued support for Ukraine amid a deepening rift between Washington and Kyiv that has raised fears the country could be left more exposed to Russian attacks heading into the winter.

Top EU officials stressed the need to keep arming Ukraine and sanctioning Russia on Friday, the second and final day of an EU summit in Brussels attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

“This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine,” said European Council President Antonio Costa, standing beside the Ukrainian leader. “This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions. Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”

The EU is hosting Zelenskyy at one of the ⁠most difficult moments for Ukraine, four-and-a-half years after neighbouring Russia invaded it.

Russian missiles and drones have rained down on Ukrainian cities daily, and Kyiv’s souring relationship with the United States has sparked fears that Washington could pull back crucial intelligence sharing and weapons support.

Arriving at the summit, Zelenskyy thanked EU leaders for their support and pointedly referred to them as “real leaders”.

That remark appeared to be a dig at US President Donald Trump, who last weekend blindsided the Ukrainian president by announcing that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities.

Zelenskyy abandoned that deal on Thursday, saying Russia had failed to live up to it, a move Trump called “a disgrace”.

Trump has also angered Ukraine by suspending sanctions on Russian oil products and striking a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow to supply large quantities of diesel to global markets.

“This diesel deal will never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets,” Zelenskyy said on the sidelines of the summit. “But it will put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war.”

He also accused the Russian leader of having no real interest in peace talks.

“Putin does not want peace talks at the moment, in any form,” Zelenskyy said. “He’s playing with words … Quite simply, it looks like a parody of a genuine desire to end the war.”

Bracing for expected winter-time attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Zelenskyy asked EU leaders for an additional 70bn euros ($79 billion) in funding next year to keep up the fight against Russia.

“The war will cost 155 billion euros [$174bn] next year. And we need at least 70 billion euros more from you – for defence, for weapons and for our resilience,” the Ukrainian president said.

“This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back.”

Al Jazeera’s Rosie Birchard, reporting from the summit in Brussels, said Zelenskyy made an “emotional plea” for European support, with air defence systems at the top of his “wish list”.

Zelenskyy appealed to European countries to dig into their own stocks to help cover Ukraine’s needs in the colder winter months, said Birchard. “But of course, that would mean some European countries potentially compromising their own national security.”

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told the Reuters news agency that the EU would probably have to provide a new loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget gap for next year.

“Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell,” Michal said.

European Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen pledged continued EU support for Ukraine through the winter.

“Russia is trying everything to destroy the energy and water infrastructure. But we stand by your side. We will support you as we did in the other winters,” she said.

Austria, however, urged caution in the debate over new, far-reaching financial commitments to Ukraine.

“There are so many figures being bandied about that we now need to put them into context, explain them and make it clear where this shortfall is coming from,” said Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker.

Al Jazeera’s Birchard said the general European solidarity for Zelenskyy was a stark difference from recent messages coming from Washington. “He is once again, at least, among friends,” she said.

However, Birchard added that some European officials were said to be appealing to Zelenskyy behind closed doors to “kind of dial down” his public criticism of Trump, which they fear could put Europeans in a tough position.

“Of course, they [European officials] want to show that they are close to Ukraine, that they are supporting Zelenskyy, but they also don’t want to antagonise the US,” she said.

Friday’s summit came as Russian strikes killed three people in Kharkiv and left hundreds of thousands of people without power in Ukraine.

The Kremlin last week said Ukraine had undermined the possibility of an immediate resumption of peace talks after hitting Moscow with drones during last month’s election.

title: Ukraine pushes Russia back on front line where Starlink has played key role
excerpt:
Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontline

A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live...
body_text:
Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontline

A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.

Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.

This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.

The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.

While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September –  and suffered few casualties in return.

The Starlink system was integrated into Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, but this week Kyiv said restrictions had been imposed on it without warning

The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".

Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.

Ukraine's military says it has liberated 277 sq km in the eastern Donbas region

He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.

This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.

Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.

Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability.

Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.

Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.

Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.

The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.

Dealer, a soldier in the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, just came off the front line

An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."

He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.

Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous".

"The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."

Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.

Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit

In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation.

"As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed."

"I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".

That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present.

"The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained.

"This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."

Nets now span roads in eastern Ukraine to protect from drones

All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.

This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin.

Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.

But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.

The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.

I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."

Additional reporting by Kostas Kallergis and Anastasiia Levchenko

title: World Series hero Miguel Rojas emotionally announces retirement after Dodgers get swept in NLCS
excerpt:
Derek Jeter, David Ortiz, Alex Rodriguez and Kevin Burkhardt reacted to the Milwaukee Brewers' sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS.

Los Angeles Dodgers World Series hero Miguel Rojas announc...
body_text:
Derek Jeter, David Ortiz, Alex Rodriguez and Kevin Burkhardt reacted to the Milwaukee Brewers' sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS.

Los Angeles Dodgers World Series hero Miguel Rojas announced his retirement from baseball Thursday at age 37.

After the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the Dodgers 6-4 to complete the sweep and advance to the World Series, an emotional Rojas said he was hanging up his spikes.

"No, I think this is it, guys," Rojas told reporters postgame. "This is it as a player. That was my last game played. That was the last time that I put these cleats on and this uniform on as a player. From now on, I'm going to start thinking about what's going to happen in my life as a baseball person."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Los Angeles Dodgers second baseman Miguel Rojas runs out a base hit during the third inning of Game 3 of the National League Championship Series between the Milwaukee Brewers and the Los Angeles Dodgers on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/Gregory Bull)

Rojas was responsible for one of the biggest swings in Dodgers history. In the ninth inning of Game 7 of the 2025 World Series, with the Dodgers trailing the Toronto Blue Jays by a run, Rojas hit a game-tying solo home run to send the game to extra innings. The Dodgers went on to win the game and secure their second consecutive World Series title.

The two-time World Series champion may have retired from playing, but he plans to remain in baseball in a different role.

"I want to start my career on the other side of the of this business and I'm looking forward to do it here, with the Los Angeles Dodgers, as well. It's really hard because I never wanted to make a big conference or anything like that but I just wanted to be clear with the guys and with everybody in this clubhouse that this was it. I'm ready to move on and start the next chapter of my career," Rojas said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Miguel Rojas hoists the Commissioner's Trophy after the Los Angeles Dodgers defeated the Toronto Blue Jays in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series at Rogers Centre in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, on Saturday, Nov. 1, 2025. (Daniel Shirey/MLB Photos via Getty Images)

Rojas began his career with the Dodgers but was traded to the Miami Marlins after his first season. He spent the next eight seasons with Miami before being traded back to Los Angeles ahead of the 2023 season.

The utility player said the last four seasons with the Dodgers have been life-changing.

"Yeah, the last the last four years here for me have changed my life and I can't be more proud of being a Los Angeles Dodger for the time that I was here and I promise the guys loyalty forever because they helped me grow. And not just as a player but as a person, as a leader, as a future coach or whatever my job is going to be in the future as a baseball man, and I'm just so happy that I got to wear this uniform until the last day of my career," Rojas said.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Los Angeles Dodgers' Miguel Rojas works out ahead of Game 1 of baseball's National League Championship Series between the Milwaukee Brewers and the Los Angeles Dodgers on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026, in Milwaukee. (AP Photo/Kyla Wolf)

"I know losing the last game of the season this year it doesn't feel the same as the last two years but there's a lot of things to be happy for and to be proud for being part of this group and trying to trying to win three times in a row. It was special and that's something that I’m going to remember forever, the good, the bads, the up and downs, is all part of the process and is all part of the journey."

In his 13-year career, Rojas was known more for his defense than his offense and was valued for his versatility across the infield. In 1,401 career games, he batted .260 with 61 home runs and 386 RBI.

Ryan Canfield is a digital production assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: Manchester Utd have ‘moved on’ from Martinez outburst, says Carrick
excerpt:
Michael Carrick said Manchester United had “moved on” from Lisandro Martinez’s outburst aimed at the club’s hierarchy this week, saying it was “really not a drama for us as a group”.

Argentina defend...
body_text:
Michael Carrick said Manchester United had “moved on” from Lisandro Martinez’s outburst aimed at the club’s hierarchy this week, saying it was “really not a drama for us as a group”.

Argentina defender Martinez took aim at the hierarchy of the struggling club following United’s 2-0 Champions League loss to Atletico Madrid on Tuesday, saying Carrick had been left with an under-strength squad.

The centre-back criticised technical director Jason Wilcox, saying he had “100 percent” expected more investment during the summer transfer window after United finished third in the Premier League last season.

It is understood Martinez has been fined for his outburst, but Carrick said he would be in United’s squad for the Premier League match at Leeds on Sunday.

“It’s done, really,” Carrick said at his pre-match news conference on Friday when asked about Martinez’s comments and his subsequent apology and punishment.

“We’ve moved on from that,” he said. “It was one of those things. He has come out and acknowledged the situation, and as a group we’ve moved on.

“It is really not a drama for us as a group. The boys have trained really well; there was a really good feeling around training this morning.”

Martinez, 28, issued an apology on Thursday, saying he had held positive talks with the club’s leadership and Carrick.

“Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity,” he said in a post on Instagram.

“The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise.”

Former United captain Roy Keane branded the situation at his former club as “a bit of a circus”.

United travel to Elland Road, the home of one of their fiercest rivals, with just two wins from nine games in all competitions this season.

They are 13th in the Premier League, with just one win from six matches and drew their last match 1-1 against 10-man Tottenham.

title: Ilhan Omar's sister skips book tour event amid week of chaos following raid on progressive's DC home
excerpt: Rep. Ilhan Omar's, D-Minn., husband, Tim Mynett, defends her immigration timeline outside their DC residence that Homeland Security Investigations raided on Monday amid a criminal fraud investigation....
body_text:
Rep. Ilhan Omar's, D-Minn., husband, Tim Mynett, defends her immigration timeline outside their DC residence that Homeland Security Investigations raided on Monday amid a criminal fraud investigation. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

ROCHESTER, Minn. — The older sister of embattled Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., who is currently on a book tour promoting a memoir about her life as a Somali immigrant, skipped a scheduled event amid the fallout from the raid on the congresswoman's home.

As Omar faces a federal government probe related to potential immigration fraud as well as a separate investigation into her financial disclosures, Sahra Noor was scheduled for a book tour stop at the University of Minnesota Rochester on Thursday night.

Noor, who came to the United States as a refugee alongside Omar and other family members in the 1990s, was reportedly subpoenaed in relation to the immigration investigation into her sister. She currently lives in Nairobi, Kenya, according to her LinkedIn page, but is on a worldwide book tour promoting her recently-released "Salt in the Snow: A Somali Immigrant Story."

Ilhan Omar wearing a patterned hijab and green scarf. (L) Sahra Noor, sister of Ilhan Omar, speaking at an event at the University of Minnesota in 2016. (Stephen Maturen/Getty Images; University of Minnesota)

ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND INSISTS HE HAS ‘NO CONCERNS’ AMID FEDERAL IMMIGRATION INVESTIGATION

Fox News Digital reached out to Noor for comment but did not hear back at time of publication.

According to a flyer, which was posted on Facebook by Rochester-based bookstore Garden Party Books, the event was scheduled for Thursday night at 6:30 p.m. It was set to be held at the Intercultural Student Center at the University of Minnesota Rochester.

When Fox News Digital arrived for the event, the space was completely empty. Fox News Digital had previously RSVP'd for the event via a QR code on the flyer and did not receive any communication that the event had been canceled, rescheduled or relocated.

Neither the University of Minnesota Rochester nor Garden Party Books returned Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The Intercultural Student Center at the University of Minnesota, Rochester, Minnesota, Thursday, October 14, 2026. Sahra Noor, sister of Rep. Ihlan Omar, was scheduled to discuss her memoir, Salt in the Snow at this location but for an undisclosed reason the event was canceled without warning. (Obtained by Fox News Digital)

Noor's absence from the book tour stop comes amid rumors that Omar fled the United States following the raid earlier this week. While the congresswoman has not been seen in public since Monday's raid, her husband snapped when asked outside the home on Wednesday whether he had a response to the rumors that she fled the country.

The flyer said that Garden Party Books, along with the University of Minnesota Bookstores and the Rochester Public Library, were "proud supporters" of the event.

It also described Noor as a "poet, storyteller and health system leader," and said the book is a "story of migration, motherhood, grief and family."

According to Noor's website, her book was officially launched during an event in a Nairobi bookstore on Aug. 13, 2026. She appeared in early September at a festival in Cape Town, South Africa to promote her work.

OMAR RAID DRAWS OMINOUS WARNING FROM VANCE AS HE BLASTS PROGRESSIVE REP'S 'RAGE' TOWARD AMERICA

Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital. (Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)

Now, she is touring in the United States. Noor held an Oct. 1 event in Minneapolis, and another five days later at the University of Minnesota. She hosted an event in St. Paul, Minnesota on Oct. 7. Her next scheduled event is at the Somali Community Cultural Innovation Hub in Seattle on Oct. 23.

Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the leading investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), executed a search warrant on Omar's home starting at around 6:00 a.m. on Monday morning.

ILHAN OMAR'S HUSBAND SNAPS OVER RUMORS SHE FLED US AFTER FEDERAL IMMIGRATION FRAUD RAID

Fox News Digital first reported Monday that the raid stems from an investigation into whether Omar or her late father, Nur Mohamed, fraudulently filled out her citizenship paperwork decades ago.

The investigation, two sources noted, could lead to the congresswoman's denaturalization.

The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Omar's phone, passport and computers were seized in the raid.

Omar has described the search as an "outrageous abuse of power" and called it an "unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."

Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.
