title: Washington school district that forced kids to hide Bibles in sealed envelopes must apologize, pay $275K
excerpt: LifeWise Academy founder Joel Penton discusses a Washington school district's restrictions on students carrying Bibles and a settlement requiring a public apology, religious liberty training and $275,...
body_text:
LifeWise Academy founder Joel Penton discusses a Washington school district's restrictions on students carrying Bibles and a settlement requiring a public apology, religious liberty training and $275,000 in attorney's fees.

A Washington state school district has agreed to publicly apologize, undergo religious liberty training and pay $275,000 in attorney's fees after a lawsuit challenged policies that required elementary school students to keep Bibles concealed in sealed envelopes, according to a Christian education organization whose CEO says children felt pressured to hide their faith.

Joel Penton, founder and CEO of LifeWise Academy, told Fox News Digital in an interview Thursday that parents described the emotional toll of the Everett School District's restrictions, which also included requiring families to submit permission slips every week for their children to attend voluntary, off-campus Bible instruction.

"I also heard from parents that their children felt like they were being told they had to hide their faith when they were told they had to put their Bibles and things in envelopes as though it was something to be ashamed of, and I know that was very hurtful as well," Penton said.

WISCONSIN STUDENT ALLEGES SCHOOL BARRED HER FROM USING BIBLE VERSE AT GRADUATION

A Washington school district forced students to hide Bibles in sealed envelopes, according to a federal lawsuit. (Getty Images)

LifeWise Academy, which provides privately funded Bible instruction to public school students during the school day with parental permission, filed suit after the Everett School District imposed restrictions that the organization argued unfairly targeted its program.

Penton said LifeWise had operated in Everett for several years, serving dozens of students and families, before the school board changed its policies.

"Then the school board changed some of their policies in some ways that were pretty transparently discriminatory and infringed on the religious liberty of our program there," Penton said. "And some of those policy changes included requiring parents, instead of simply signing a permission slip one time for the entire semester, the entire year, they were requiring them to hand-bring in a permission slip each and every week, which was quite onerous."

Penton said they were told they were not allowed to participate at some of the community fairs, which he claimed other student organizations were able to participate in.

TEXAS BOARD OF EDUCATION APPROVES REQUIRED READING LIST WITH BIBLE PASSAGES FOR 5 MILLION STUDENTS

Everett School District told Fox News Digital that there had been no changes to the policy and student release guidelines were "updated to comply with the terms of the settlement." (iStock)

"And then they also told students that if they received any worksheets or even a Bible at our program, when they came back to the school, that those had to come back in sealed envelopes so that other students wouldn't be exposed to them," Penton said.

He argued that the weekly permission requirement threatened the program's ability to operate.

"We knew at least with the permission slip policy that it was meant to effectively shut down the program, that one of the reasons students, parents enroll their students is because of how practical and convenient it is for them to receive Bible education during school hours as part of their school day," Penton said. "And now to tell them that they had to personally bring in a permission slip each and every week just made it really impractical for a lot of parents, and I know there are many who are frustrated about that."

Penton said LifeWise initially attempted to resolve the dispute directly with school officials and later through an attorney before filing suit.

EXCLUSIVE: INDIANA SCHOOL COUNSELOR FIRED FOR SPEAKING OUT ON GENDER IDENTITY POLICY SETTLES LAWSUIT FOR $200K

The settlement announced by LifeWise Academy requires, among other things, religious liberty training for school board members and $275,000 in attorney's fees, according to the organization. (Brian A. Jackson/South Florida Sun Sentinel)

In April, a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction against the district, according to LifeWise.

The settlement announced Wednesday by LifeWise Academy requires changes to district policies, religious liberty training for school board members, a public written apology posted on the district's website for six months and $275,000 in attorney's fees, according to the organization.

The announcement of the settlement quoted a statement from the district which said, "The District recognizes that comments made at various Board meetings that concerned LifeWise, including by Directors, were offensive and hurtful to the families participating in LifeWise programming. For that, the District and its Board of Directors offer a sincere apology."

In a statement posted on their website, Everett Public Schools said, "Parents and guardians have the right to choose to seek the release of their students during the school day for religious-related activities or instruction that occurs off school property for part of the school day pursuant to District Policy 2340 and Procedure 2340P. The policy and procedures align with both Washington State (RCW 28A.600.025) and federal law, with which the district is required to comply. The procedure allows students to be excused for a portion of the school day, provided the instruction is conducted off-site and does not disrupt their regular classroom instructional time."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Everett School District for comment and was referred back to the district's statement, with the school district saying, "There were no changes to the policy. The Student Release Guidelines have been updated to comply with the terms of the settlement."

Rachel del Guidice is a culture reporter for Fox News covering the intersection of politics, faith, family, and American culture.

title: ‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: what the reviewers say about NAZA documentary
excerpt:
Film interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza receives widespread praise around the world

Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary NAZA as a “b...
body_text:
Film interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza receives widespread praise around the world

Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary NAZA as a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”.

NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, was released in UK cinemas this week and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.

The investigative documentary, which contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders speaking anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, has received widespread praise.

In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus”.

British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”. The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”.

Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region. As a work of cinema, it is exemplary. As a work of journalism, it is inarguable. As a document, it is an indictment.”

The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”. The Los Angeles Times says NAZA is a “stone-cold frightening” film that “burns the conscience”. And in New York magazine, it is described as “one of the most important films of our time”.

The Hollywood Reporter praises NAZA as a “sober and thoroughly documented bombshell of an expose” that “leaves one with a deadening feeling, as if humanity may have lost all hope”. The Toronto Star says “NAZA is heartbreaking but essential viewing, questioning the systems that cause and quantify civilian death in modern warfare”.

The Spanish outlet El Mundo hailed NAZA as “the film of our time, a superb, electrifying, and devastating documentary about the systematic model of annihilation of the Palestinian people” that ultimately “points the finger at us. At night, in silence.”

The French newspaper Le Monde says the film “has the effect of an uppercut that leaves the viewer stunned”, while the Danish culture magazine Soundvenue calls NAZA a “soul-crushing testimony to the genocide in Gaza” that is an “example of how the world increasingly seems like a dystopia”.

The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”.

When the film opened in Italy last month, it topped the charts. The Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera says NAZA lasts “only 80 minutes, but no more is needed: the ‘scientific’ coldness with which the interviewees reconstruct how they are destroying Gaza is something unforgettable”.

The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.

Various bodies, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize.

title: Fever star Sophie Cunningham calls Angel Reese dodging $500 fine for technical foul 'absolutely insane'
excerpt: WNBA player Sophie Cunningham faces intense backlash after defending women's sports, prompting a columnist to urge the Indiana Fever to drop her. Fox News contributor Kat Timpf and podcast host Kenned...
body_text:
WNBA player Sophie Cunningham faces intense backlash after defending women's sports, prompting a columnist to urge the Indiana Fever to drop her. Fox News contributor Kat Timpf and podcast host Kennedy join Ainsley Earhardt to discuss the controversy, noting that 80% of the country agrees with her position. They also preview a new episode of 'the Girls' podcast.

With the WNBA Finals set to begin on Saturday afternoon between the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream, all the chatter is around which of these franchises will win their first championship since joining the league.

For Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham, though, her focus is on a different issue.

During the Dream's series-clinching win in Game 3 against the New York Liberty back on October 9, a situation unfolded following a foul in which Atlanta forward Angel Reese followed Liberty guard Sabrina Ionescu after the latter had committed an illegal screen.

Sabrina Ionescu of the New York Liberty handles the ball against Angel Reese of the Atlanta Dream during the first quarter of Game 2 of the WNBA playoffs semifinals at State Farm Arena in Atlanta on Oct. 7, 2026. (Getty Images)

Reese followed Ionescu down the court shouting "you can't do that" at the four-time WNBA All-Star.

No technical foul was called, which incensed Cunningham.

FEVER STAR SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM TELLS ACES' A'JA WILSON TO 'GROW UP' IN RESPONSE TO HER PLAYOFF MELTDOWN

The Fever guard mentioned on her "No Hesitation" podcast that Reese avoiding the technical and subsequent $500 fine that is usually tacked on to a playoff tech was "absolutely ridiculous."

"If you're going to chase someone down the court and get in someone's ear, that should be a tech. Anytime," Cunningham said. "It's going to be a tech in the regular season. Now, if she were to stay on her side and just kind of yell and say something, I'm all for that. But the fact that she didn't get a tech on that, I think that's absolutely insane."

CAITLIN CLARK CALLS FOR FULL-TIME WNBA REFEREES AS OFFICIATING FAILURES MOUNT IN 2026

Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham celebrates a three-point basket Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026, during a game at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

She wasn't the only one to share this sentiment, though, as ESPN WNBA analyst Rebecca Lobo mentioned on the broadcast that Reese should have been hit with a technical foul as the incident unfolded.

While Cunningham was clearly miffed at the circumstances, she did mention that she respects the fact that Reese had her teammate's back in that situation.

ANGEL REESE REVEALS 'EMBARRASSING' TRAINING CAMP STORY AFTER REACHING WNBA FINALS WITH ATLANTA DREAM

The problem with not calling that first technical foul, though, is that a few minutes later, Reese was T'd up after standing chest-to-chest with Jonquel Jones after blocking her layup attempt into the stands.

Two technical fouls in the same game would have resulted in an ejection of Reese, and could have changed the game in favor of the Liberty.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Cunningham didn't like the technical that was actually called on Reese, calling it "good playoff basketball," but did take exception to the gap between the two calls, characterizing it as "weird and inconsistent."

Reese is sitting on two technical fouls heading into the Finals, and two more within the span of the seven-game series would result in a one-game suspension.

Angel Reese of the Atlanta Dream celebrates during Game 3 of the semifinals against the New York Liberty on Oct. 9, 2026, at Barclays Center Arena in Brooklyn, N.Y. (NBAE)

Reese and Cunningham's teammate, Caitlin Clark, have a history of hard fouls and competitive banter between the two.

With that in mind, some credit has to go to Cunningham for being measured and fair in her assessment of Reese's fouls.

title: Josh Brolin says he became a full-time stock trader after Hollywood stopped calling
excerpt:
The 'Ransom Canyon" actor tells Fox News Digital he tried to be there for his kids as much as possible when they were growing up, but it can be hard as an actor.

Josh Brolin said he wasn’t taken seri...
body_text:
The 'Ransom Canyon" actor tells Fox News Digital he tried to be there for his kids as much as possible when they were growing up, but it can be hard as an actor.

Josh Brolin said he wasn’t taken seriously as an actor until 2007’s Oscar-winning "No Country for Old Men" — and in the years before landing the movie, he had a short career as a full-time stock trader.

The 58-year-old son of actor James Brolin told Theo Von on his "This Past Weekend" podcast that despite early success on "The Goonies," his career in Hollywood was going nowhere.

Before he was cast as Brand in "The Goonies," he said he went to "350 auditions," and people told him, "It's not for you."

'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' STAR SAYS CHILD ACTORS GET 'DROPPED' AFTER HOLLYWOOD FAME FADES

Josh Brolin said he worked as a stock trader full-time in his 30s when his Hollywood career was floundering. (Getty Images)

He said the '80s classic was his first time ever in front of a camera, admitting, "I ruined the first day of shooting 'cause I couldn’t stop laughing" because he was so nervous.

Steven Spielberg told him to "take a breath" on the first day, because "we need to get through this."

GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'

Soon after making "The Goonies," he went to New York to study acting and do theater. He said that he "took it seriously," and he "had 22 years of taking it seriously because nobody was interested until really I did ‘No Country,’ and then ‘No Country’ kind of changed s---."

During that period, Brolin said he worked as a landscaper for a year and then became a stock trader when he was 30, "for almost five years full-time."

"I was really good at it," he admitted, explaining that he worked from home using three screens, "four tabs per screen."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Josh Brolin, center, stands with the cast of "The Goonies." (Getty Images)

He said he did both swing trading and day trading.

BRAD PITT, MARGOT ROBBIE WORKED FAST FOOD JOBS AS EVA LONGORIA SAYS ‘EVERY KID NEEDS TO'

"I made more money in those four years, really … than I had made in 20 years acting. But I didn’t really make hardly anything acting."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Josh Brolin promotes "No Country for Old Men" with Kelly Macdonald and Javier Bardem at the Cannes Film Festival. (WireImage)

Even after he found critical acclaim in the industry, the money wasn’t blowing him away.

For "No Country for Old Men," he said he was paid $100,000, "so I cleared what, $30,000? That’s not considered a great year."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Josh Brolin and the cast of "Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps" ring the opening bell at the NASDAQ MarketSite in New York City in 2010. (WireImage)

But his Hollywood career began to turn around quickly after that.

While filming "No Country for Old Men," Brolin said he sent in an audition tape for "American Gangster" with his 16-year-old son playing Denzel Washington’s part.

"And that’s the last audition I ever did," he said.

Brolin is now starring in the thriller "Whalefall," about a diver who is swallowed by a whale. Brolin plays the main character's estranged father.

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy
excerpt:
Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White House

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access...
body_text:
Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White House

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House.

Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia.

The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president, Donald Trump.

Hours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised ⁠Zelenskyy, after an purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.

“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.”

Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having the biggest impact on diesel export volumes, although the Ukraine war was also significant.

Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying above 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed.

Speaking after meeting EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy said that Starshield had not yet returned to normal.

“Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities,” Zelenskyy said. “Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.”

Reuters on Friday reported that the order to throttle Starshield had come from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a western official briefed on the matter. They did not identify the White House official who had made the decision, but said the Pentagon had been informed that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military had to be slowed.

Zelenskyy called it a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise” that speeds had been reduced on Starlink, which Ukraine uses to support its most effective air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones.

Starlink is produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, but controlled by the US government.

When Zelenskyy arrived for talks with EU leaders, he was applauded by the heads of state and government of the bloc’s 27 countries. Zelenskyy later said he had heard “only support”, when asked about reports that European leaders had asked him to dial down his criticism of Trump.

According to a transcript of his remarks, he told EU leaders that the war would cost €155bn in 2027. “And we need at least €70 bn more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” he said. “This is a realistic amount.”

The EU is currently giving Ukraine regular payments from a €90bn funding plan agreed last December that was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s civilian and military needs for 2026-27. The remaining third was to be filled by other “international partners”, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan.

The realisation that Kyiv again risks a financial crunch has put Russia’s €210bn assets frozen inside the EU back on the table. The EU takes the profits from those assets to support Ukraine, but last year decided against using the funds themselves, instead opting for an EU-backed €90bn loan.

Belgium, which hosts the vast majority of the Russian funds, remains strongly opposed to using the frozen assets, fearing it will be left to carry the financial burden if the plan goes wrong. But Zelenskyy said there could be an alternative.

“We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war,” he said.

The European Commission, a strong backer of last year’s rejected frozen assets plan, has been reluctant to propose new variants – such as an EU-controlled custodian – because it fears running into same opposition from Belgium and other sceptical member states.

Before the summit, Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever, said Zelenskyy would “probably look everybody straight in the eye and say: thank you for the €90bn, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing”.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU had supported Trump’s energy ceasefire, “but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute” and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions and adding: “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.”

title: Gaza malnutrition and starvation at ‘catastrophic’ levels: Health Ministry
excerpt: Malnutrition and starvation rates in Gaza have reached “catastrophic” levels, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, despite a United States-brokered “ceasefire” that aims in part to allow m...
body_text:
Malnutrition and starvation rates in Gaza have reached “catastrophic” levels, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, despite a United States-brokered “ceasefire” that aims in part to allow more food and medical supplies to enter the Strip as Palestinians face famine.

At least 466 Palestinians have died of malnutrition and starvation since 2024, with children accounting for one-third of the deaths, the Gaza Health Ministry said on Friday, in a statement released for World Food Day.

Elderly Palestinians accounted for the largest share of malnutrition-related deaths in the Strip, with 189 deaths, representing 40.5 percent of the total. The ministry said 11 percent of older people went without a meal for an entire day and 48 percent reduced portions so their families could eat.

The ministry estimated that 74,200 children would require treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027.

Malnutrition was also driving up rates of anaemia among pregnant women to 61 percent in 2026, up from 41 percent before the war began in October 2023. Nearly 4,000 pregnancy losses were recorded in the first half of 2026, more than three times the number recorded in the preceding six months.

More than 1.4 million Palestinians – 67 percent of Gaza’s population – are projected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026 as winter months approach, the ministry warned.

The United Nations children’s agency, UNICEF, said that gains in tackling Gaza’s hunger crisis were fragile. It warned that the situation could worsen due to disruption of supplies entering Strip, and urged that crossings remain open.

A UNICEF report ⁠published on Friday found that while the so-called “ceasefire” between Israel and Hamas last October ⁠had allowed more humanitarian aid and commercial supplies to enter, acute malnutrition remains a risk.

The report said scaled-up food and nutrition response and the easing of restrictions on the entry of food and nutrition ⁠supplies helped to avert a prolonged famine after it was declared in August 2025.

Speaking to reporters in Geneva, UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires said the flow of both commercial and humanitarian supplies must remain predictable and continuous.

“The impact on children obviously will be felt if this situation is not resolved,” he said. “We can’t go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods, and services that they require.”

Israel said on Wednesday that no commercial goods had entered the Strip in days, blaming the supply shortages on a tax dispute between local merchants and Hamas. The Palestinian group dismissed Israel’s claims as “baseless” while Gaza’s Government Media Office condemned Israel’s “blatant disinformation campaign and false statement”.

Israel’s move to halt supplies has cut off a vital source of ⁠food and other goods in a territory where most depend on humanitarian assistance after three years of war, repeated displacement and stringent Israeli restrictions on aid deliveries.

Even before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in 2023, an Israeli land, sea and air blockade restricted the flow of food, clean water, fuel and medical supplies from entering the Strip.

Gaza’s Health Ministry has called for international action to ensure unrestricted entry of food and medicine into the Strip. It also called for support to revive local food production.

title: Target pensions or welfare, not banks, IMF tells John Healey
excerpt:
Supporters of planned tax, however, say banks were bailed out by taxpayers during financial crisis and can afford to pay more now

John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budget

The Internation...
body_text:
Supporters of planned tax, however, say banks were bailed out by taxpayers during financial crisis and can afford to pay more now

John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budget

The International Monetary Fund has urged John Healey to target savings on pensions and welfare, instead of taxing Britain’s banks at the budget later this month.

Helge Berger, deputy director of the IMF’s European department, was asked about bank taxes after the Guardian revealed Healey plans to tap the sector for additional revenue.

Berger replied that given the UK’s current high tax-to-GDP ratio, it might be better to “put the emphasis” on cuts.

He said if additional tax revenue were needed, reforming property taxes or VAT might be a good place to start.

He added: “Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP – historically, for Britain, a high number – then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal [spending] side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.”

As examples, he highlighted the pensions triple lock – which Labour has already said it will reform – and “better targeting [of] social benefits”, adding: “I think that’s where you would put the emphasis, rather than the tax that you mentioned.”

Berger was speaking in Bangkok, where the IMF has held its annual meetings this week.

City lobbyists have been out in full force, warning the government that higher taxes could force banks to throttle lending, hitting the economy and even forcing some lenders to move jobs and operations abroad.

In a letter sent to Healey and copied to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, on 12 October, days before news of the planned tax hike broke, the chief executive of UK Finance, David Postings, shared research commissioned by the lobby group.

It suggested that reversing Tory cuts to the bank surcharge – taking it back to 8% from 3% – would leave annual UK GDP £1.2bn lower in real terms by 2029-30 than it would have otherwise been.

He said it would also see banks issue fewer business loans and mortgages, with lending likely to be £10.4bn lower in 2029-2030 than if the surcharge was held at 3%.

“The UK’s banking sector already makes a vital contribution to the wider economy,” Postings’ letter said. “To sustain this vital contribution, the budget should avoid any increases in bank-specific taxes, as this would risk constraining the sector’s ability to lend and invest.”

However, TUC analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the Treasury has already lost out on £6bn over the three years since the surcharge cut came into force in 2023.

At the same time, banks have been reporting strong profits, largely off the back of high interest rates, with bosses subsequently increasing banker bonus pots and handing billions of pounds to shareholders.

Collectively, the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds – reported £29.2bn in profits over the first six months of the year, with almost half, £13.7bn, pledged to investors through dividends and share buybacks. Over the past five years, those banks have raked in £200bn in pre-tax profits.

Author and former banker Philip Augar said the banks were “enjoying boom conditions”, partly due to good management but partly due to economic conditions “not of their own making”. He said there was room for a “moderate increase in taxation” that would raise about £2bn to £3bn a year.

“The prime minister has said that the burden of taxation has to fall on those with the broader shoulders, and at the moment, it’s hard to think of a sector where the shoulders are much broader than the banking sector,” Augar told the BBC’s Today programme on Friday.

While banks could not expect interest rates benefits to continue forever, Augar said that banks – including those that were bailed out in the 2008 financial crisis – could not have it both ways.

“Banking is cyclical, it’s true. But when it hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out,” Augar said. “When it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment. Banks can’t be too big to fail and too big to tax.”

Some banks have threatened to pull investment, and potentially jobs, from the UK if it hikes taxes, with lobby groups noting smaller overall tax charges in rival financial centres like Frankfurt, Dublin and Amsterdam.

Jamie Dimon, who heads up the largest bank in the US, JP Morgan, said in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile towards banks.

But Augar said the government needed to see past the bluster. “There seems to have been a coordinated campaign by the big international banks who have businesses in Britain – JP Morgan, Citigroup, Santander, HSBC and others.

“But they always say this, [and] they rarely move. I think that if the chancellor judges this right, with a moderate increase in taxation or some other form of getting money from the banks, then the business will remain in the UK.”

title: Zelenskyy holds press conference after talks with EU leaders over breakdown in US relationship – Europe live
excerpt:
Ukraine president also says Starlink speeds not fully restored and Kyiv working with France on other options

Zelenskyy gets asked about Trump’s comments that he is more difficult to deal with than Pu...
body_text:
Ukraine president also says Starlink speeds not fully restored and Kyiv working with France on other options

Zelenskyy gets asked about Trump’s comments that he is more difficult to deal with than Putin (11:09).

He says that in his meetings with Trump he always found topics for discussion and decisions.

“I’m only standing up for Ukraine’s interests,” he says, responding to Russian attacks.

“And no matter how Russia would like to limit all of our rights, it’s clear that we do have a right to defend ourselves.”

He says Putin “does not seek negotiations in any format,” but only “playing these games of words.” “He does not want the war to end,” he says, saying Putin’s actions are a “parody” of efforts to end the war.

He says that’s why he cannot accept any diesel deals with the US, because they will then be followed by gas agreements or other attempts to lift sanctions on Russia or its frozen assets, banking system, chemical industry, certain Russian individuals.

“If I don’t stand up to this, if I don’t defend it, who else will do this diplomatically?”

Asked about his relationship with Hungary’s Magyar (13:08), Zelenskyy says it was “a very good meeting” on the economy, logistics, energy.

He says he is “not against” meeting the Hungarian PM in Budapest next.

Zelenskyy gets asked if he heard any criticism from fellow leaders to his response to the US deal with Russia on diesel.

He says he “heard … only support,” and he is “grateful to them for this.”

He says the diesel deal caught Ukraine by surprise, and he believes Ukraine “should be aware of these things.”

He says despite all of that Ukraine is ready to support an energy ceasefire, but “it all depends on Russia and they do not want it.”

“And if there is no energy ceasefire, give us anti-ballistic missiles so that I can protect my energy facilities – … not too many, but for the period … of the diesel deal.”

He says Ukrainian negotiators are in touch with their US counterparts, and “in the coming days, they will arrange a meeting at a certain level,” and they will keep discussing it.

Zelenskyy gets directly asked if Ukraine is hitting refineries in Russia.

He says he “usually don’t communicate” the details of Ukraine’s military operations, but says “the main rule of our operations is to respond.”

Earlier he said Europe is “making certain steps” to have its own track in peace negotiations, but he didn’t offer more details on that.

Zelenskyy says that Ukraine’s requests for further help ahead of this winter cover “the bare minimum” needed.

He says it’s unclear what Ukraine could get, but he is confident that European countries have enough interceptors to share and “go through this winter.”

He also says the focus is on producing a new anti-ballistic system and make it “quicker to produce, cheaper to produce” and then share with the rest of Europe.

Zelenskyy then gets asked about media reports that Ukraine is running out of Patriot interceptors and its reliance on Starlink.

He acknowledges that Ukraine is “not a priority destination” for deliveries funded by Europe, but thanks for all help it can get.

“We are picking them up where we can: one or two here, five there, ten there, arranging all of this and bringing them to Ukraine,” he says.

On Starlink, he says Ukraine “is working with some countries, including France” on additional capabilities.

Zelenskyy also addresses the issue of intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

He says “many countries are sharing their intel with us, … dozens of countries.”

But he then gets asked again for a straight clarification on what is the status of both Starlink (or its military version, Starshield) and US intel.

On Starlink, he says “certain speed levels are needed” for its military to work properly – not for “deep strikes inside Russia,” but for its defence operations, particularly against Russian jet-powered drones.

“This is why it was a very dangerous and unpleasant surprise,” he says.

“Starlink was not turned off, but the speed limits were lowered … and we were incapable of shooting down some Shahed drones, and were no longer able to use one of the tools to protect our population,” he says.

Jet-powered Shaheds move at 400 km/h, and the speed limits were reduced to 70 km/h, he says.

He says the technology is also used for “mid-range strikes against military targets,” and for logistics deliveries.

“Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities. Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.”

The briefing kicks off with Zelenskyy getting a question about Russian frozen assets and Belgium’s opposition to the issue.

He says by thanking Belgium for hosting the summit and for his meetings with PM de Wever and the Belgian king, Philippe. Ukraine expects additional F-16 from Belgium to be delivered by the end of the year.

Turning to frozen assets, he says “of course” he is raising this issue again.

He says Ukraine “would want to receive these funds in a certain format” and wants them to be safeguarded from Russia, “because we know very clearly that they want to bring these assets back.”

Zelenskyy is finally here to brief the media after his EU talks in Brussels.

I will bring you all the key lines here, but you can also watch along here:

We are still waiting for Zelenskyy to show up to his press conference, but in the meantime we have just heard from Hungary’s Péter Magyar after his first meeting with the Ukrainian president.

The pair have a long list of tricky topics to discuss given Hungary’s tense relations with Ukraine under the previous government of Viktor Orbán, including the issue of minority rights for Hungarians in Ukraine, which is critical to Kyiv’s ambitions of joining the EU.

But the noises coming from that meeting are positive.

In a statement after the talks, Magyar welcomed the Ukrainian parliament’s adoption of a new law on minority education as “a first step towards restoring mutual trust,” and the two sides will “continue consultations … at the ministerial level.”

“We agreed that it is in the interest of both countries to place their political and economic relations on a new foundation,” he said.

In sharp contrast to his predecessor, Magyar also declared his strong solidarity with Zelenskyy “in the face of inhumane Russian aggression against his country.”

“Hungary stands ready to provide assistance, through all available diplomatic means, towards achieving an immediate ceasefire and a lasting peace,” he said.

Back to Brussels, we are expecting to hear from Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy shortly, as he is about to deliver a press conference after his talks with EU leaders.

I will bring you all the key lines here when he steps up to the podium.

Separately, Italy is struggling with technical issues affecting the data transmission network for air traffic control, with lengthy delays at airports across the country affecting thousands of passengers.

Transport minister Matteo Salvini is “monitoring” the situation closely, his ministry said, with particular focus on ensuring the safety of operations, La Repubblica reported.

The air navigation operator ENAV ruled out any “malicious activity,” and said the disruption was due to technical issues with the system managed by telecom operator TIM, Corriere della Sera said.

Italy and Spain are reported to be close to dropping temporary border controls, introduced after the migration crisis in Ceuta in late August.

The move, reported in the Italian and Spanish press, was reportedly discussed on the sidelines of the ongoing EU summit in Brussels, with Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez and Italian PM Giorgia Meloni meeting on Thursday night.

The current thinking includes Italy extending its measures for seven days to align their expiry date with the Spanish restriction, when both would get lifted simultaneously on 22 October, El País reported.

Italy first suspended Schengen arrangements with Spain in late July, much to criticism from Spain.

In their doorstep comments, EU leaders also called for Europe to do more on reducing Ukraine’s dependence on the US Starlink satellite communications system.

The bloc’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Europe did not have a readily available alternative to technology controlled by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, AFP reported.

“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in (the) short term Europe can’t replace this capability,” Kallas said before the talks.

“Starlink is the key for Ukraine actually to fight or fight back,” Latvian prime minister Andris Kulbergs told reporters.

Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten said he had discussed with French president Emmanuel Macron “how we, as Europeans, can provide more of these kinds of services in the not too distant future”.

Bloomberg reported that the European Union will look to fast-track antitrust approvals for a rival European project.

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he discussed financial support for Ukraine with the presidents of the European Commission and European Council on the margins of the EU summit in Brussels.

“I had a good meeting with the President of the European Council, António Costa @eucopresident, and the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen @vonderleyen.

Right now, there are no signals from Russia that it is ready to end its war. The signals it is sending point to something entirely different and certainly do not bring peace any closer. After overnight Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, Russia carried out a horrific strike on Kharkiv this morning. Two people have already been reported killed. My condolences to their families and loved ones. Seventeen others were injured. Russia also struck a shopping mall in Rivne and energy facilities in four regions.

European leadership is needed to ensure that people’s lives are sufficiently protected from this Russian terror. We appreciate that everything we agree on is implemented promptly. Today, we discussed further assistance, first and foremost for our energy and air defense needs. We talked about support for our financial resilience, including for next year, and coordinated our work on the European integration track. It is important that new negotiating clusters were opened this week. We are working to open the remaining two by the end of the year. Thank you, António! Thank you, Ursula! Thank you, EU!”

title: Burnham says he wants to devolve power so places can ‘change things for themselves’ – UK politics live
excerpt:
The prime minister is speaking about devolving decision-making powers away from both Westminster and Holyrood towards regions and towns

Andy Burnham has begun his speech in North Lanarkshire, Scotlan...
body_text:
The prime minister is speaking about devolving decision-making powers away from both Westminster and Holyrood towards regions and towns

Andy Burnham has begun his speech in North Lanarkshire, Scotland. You can watch live below as we bring you the latest lines:

Burham has finished his speech, which lasted about 35 minutes. I could just about hear him on the hot mic saying “sorry that went on a bit” as he shook someone’s hand off camera.

The prime minister said he is making a “serious and genuine offer” to the Scottish government to put more control “in the hands of local people”.

double quotation markWe need to look at the resources and decision-making powers that sit at the regional level in Scotland, so that no Scottish city regions are left behind.

I know the Scottish government has announced a long term programme for local government reform.

But if you ask me, we’ve got to move faster … if we don’t move now, Scotland could lose out.

There is a risk that some of the towns and cities become underpowered when some of the towns and cities of the north of England are going the other way and starting to power up. I don’t want to see that as prime minister.”

Burnham spoke of Ravenscraig, once the pride of Scotland’s steel industry that employed tens of thousands of people before it closed in 1992.

double quotation markWhen it closed, it wasn’t just a works that shut, it was a whole community which saw the pillars underneath it just taken away, collapsed beneath it.

That was a decision taken hundreds of miles away without any real consequences for what that would mean for people here, taken by people who would never have to live with those consequences, or see those consequences.

Every day and more than 30 years on, I know that work is still ongoing to fill the Raven’s Craig site, such was the hole that it left.

He recalled how the mining community in the Lancashire coalfield in Leigh were equally let down by decisions in Westminster when it shut down.

double quotation markI was the MP there for 16 years from the early 2000s, just after the pits had shut in the 1990s. It broke my heart to see the old miners shuffling into my surgery, carrying oxygen bottles, still struggling to get compensation for the damage that was done to their lungs.

It pained me to drive past the wasteland around Bickershaw Colliery, one of the last pits to close in Leigh. Nobody asked Leigh what was going to come next either.

You know, no one in Whitehall went to Leigh and said, well, here’s what we’re going to do with transition … and this is the way that the UK has been run in our lifetimes, and it’s what needs to change.

It took so much from Motherwell and its people in terms of the building of Britain. And it took so much from Leigh in terms of the powering of Britain, and then just abandoned them when life moved on.”

Burnham said he wants to give more power to people and places in order for them to “change things for themselves”.

double quotation markI care about Scotland a lot, and I am coming today with a big offer and in search of common ground.

When I walked into Downing Street in July, I said I wanted to do politics differently. Place first, not party first. Honestly, I meant it, and I arrive here in that spirit because people in Scotland, in my view, deserve better from politicians and politics.

I want to show that politics can can be better and we can work in a different way.

Lots of cheers from the young audience after Burnham concedes he is in the “true north”.

“Please don’t tell anyone in Manchester,” he joked.

Andy Burnham has begun his speech in North Lanarkshire, Scotland. You can watch live below as we bring you the latest lines:

We should be hearing from Andy Burnham shortly, as Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, said he will “of course” work with the prime minister if he wants to devolve more powers to Scotland.

“The prime minister is very welcome in Scotland and I’ll be interested to hear what he’s got to say,” the SNP leader said, according to the Press Association.

He added: “I’ve got a track record throughout my political life of working to make sure as many powers as possible are exercised here in Scotland.”

Meanwhile, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is also in Scotland today, where she is visiting the Malcolm Group logistics company near Glasgow and browsing its collection of trucks. Here she is in front of one such truck adorned with a giant mural of Braveheart:

Also today, the Ofsted schools inspectorate has offered schools a new complaints review service, in an effort to placate critics who say its inspections place headteachers and staff in England under immense stress and excessive workloads.

Ofsted’s proposal unveiled today comes after the National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) and the National Governors Association (NGA) separately called for changes in Ofsted’s leadership and culture.

The two groups were adding their voices to those calling for an overhaul of Ofsted and its school inspection regime, including the Association of School and College Leaders and the National Education Union.

In the wake of the death of headteacher Ruth Perry after an Ofsted inspection, Labour pledged to reform school inspections. But the new framework introduced by Ofsted last year has been criticised for making matters worse.

A survey by the NGA reported one governor as saying they saw their school’s senior staff “break down routinely throughout the two days” of inspection, while another said: “The outcome was fair but the process was brutal.”

The NAHT’s national executive said in a statement:

double quotation markThis is no longer about further amendment to a bankrupt framework.

The leadership and culture of Ofsted must change so that the government and the sector can engage, in an atmosphere of restored trust and good faith, to create an inspection system that is trusted by the sector, valued by parents and the government.”

Ofsted said it will establish the new independent complaints review next year to hear challenges from schools dissatisfied with the outcomes of Ofsted’s existing internal complaints service.

But Andy Jordan, the Association of School and College Leaders’ inspection and accountability specialist, said “much more” needs to be done to restore confidence in Ofsted.

“It’s important to realise that this will not address the central issue of why so many schools feel compelled to complain in the first place,” he said.

Scottish independence is “bigger than any party”, the Scottish Green co-leader, Gillian Mackay, said. But she cautioned that votes from Green and SNP supporters will not be enough to win a second referendum.

Mackay is due to speak at the SNP’s annual party conference in Aberdeen tomorrow on a panel discussion about Scottish independence, which has not gone down well with some SNP members, according to the Press Association.

Still, Mackay said she was “delighted” to be speaking at the SNP conference, adding she would be “discussing how we can best take the independence movement forward”.

But she stressed: “Independence is bigger than any party. SNP supporters and Green supporters alone are not enough to secure a sustained pro-independence majority and to secure the referendum that we need.

“We need to reach beyond our own parties, bring more people with us and build the broadest possible movement for Scotland’s right to choose our own future.”

John Healey is poised to tax Britain’s banks in his 28 October budget, to help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, the Guardian understands.

The chancellor is in Bangkok, where the International Monetary Fund has praised the UK’s progress towards balancing the books, urging him to “stay the course”.

To keep the Treasury’s deficit reduction plans on track in the face of rising government borrowing costs, the Guardian understands Healey has decided to tap the financial sector for additional revenue.

One option understood to be under discussion – reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt – would raise upwards of £2bn a year.

Lenders have been logging strong earnings on the back of rising interest rates, with the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds Banking Group – alone having generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years.

Thinktanks and trade unions have repeatedly urged Healey to tax Britain’s banks more heavily, an option considered but rejected by his predecessor Rachel Reeves, who was wary of deterring future investment.

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), said: “Britain’s big four banks are making a billion pounds a week, while bonuses have hit a post-crash record. These are bumper profits, driven by high interest rates and households’ mortgage misery. It’s time to make sure banks pay their fair share.”

Good morning and welcome to our UK politics live blog. Prime minister Andy Burnham is in Scotland today where he is expected to invite Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, to collaborate on devolving decision-making powers away from both Westminster and Holyrood and pushing control further down to Scottish regions and towns.

The newswires have reported an extract of his speech, which he is expected to deliver in Lanarkshire around midday:

double quotation markDuring my first week in office, I told the first minister that I wanted to work with him to spread opportunities to communities across Scotland’s regions and cities.

Through No10 North, we are rewiring the state and I want to make sure regions in Scotland are fully part of this.

This is me making an offer to the Scottish government. With us working together, there is no limit to what we can achieve for the Scottish people.”

Burnham’s visit coincides with the SNP’s annual party conference in Aberdeen, which the party has said will launch the biggest pro-independence campaign since the 2014 referendum.

The prime minister has repeatedly ruled out another independence referendum, but he has been accused of hypocrisy by the SNP for proposing to reopen the debate on Brexit and re-examining the UK’s relationship with the EU.

“That hypocrisy is there for all to see and I think the Scottish electorate will take a pretty dim view of it,” SNP minister Stephen Flynn told the Press Association.

He added: “Mr Burnham wants power pushed out of Westminster – so do we.

“But let’s make sure that power and that decision making is taken by the Scottish people and they have the opportunity to do so in an independence referendum.”

Young people who rely on benefits will be given less money in exchange for more intensive health and employment support under plans for a separate youth welfare system, the Financial Times reported. Alan Milburn, who is leading a major review into Britain’s youth jobs crisis, will recommend benefits for young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) be delivered through a different process, sources told the newspaper.

Reform’s Robert Jenrick has responded to claims made by his colleague Sarah Pochin that the party is “chauvinistic”, after she was caught by an undercover ITV news reporter complaining about the party’s culture. “That’s not my experience of Reform,” Jenrick told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.

John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the UK banking sector in his 28 October budget, the Guardian understands. One option on the table is reversing former Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt’s 2023 cut to the bank profit surcharge, from 3% back to 8%. You can read more on this story here:

title: Why is China buying up gold?
excerpt: China is increasing its gold reserves in a bid to reduce its dependence on US dollar assets and protect against financial and geopolitical risks, analysts say, while households are turning to the prec...
body_text:
China is increasing its gold reserves in a bid to reduce its dependence on US dollar assets and protect against financial and geopolitical risks, analysts say, while households are turning to the precious metal amid uncertainty over the domestic economy.

The People’s Bank of China reported buying gold for a 23rd consecutive month in September, when the country’s central bank also made its largest monthly purchase in nearly three years. The sustained buying points to a longer-term effort to spread risk associated with its vast reserves, experts say.

Among concerns is high US debt and Western governments’ freezing of assets, which has highlighted the inherent risk in holding money overseas, particularly for emerging market and Global South economies. Gold bought and stored domestically offers protection against that risk because access does not depend on the will of another government.

But central bank buying and household demand for gold in China have different drivers. While Beijing is managing its financial exposure, private investors are seeking somewhere to preserve their savings. Here is what we know.

China’s central bank added approximately 23 tonnes of gold in September, bringing its reported holdings to about 2,410 tonnes, according to the World Gold Council. That was its largest monthly purchase since October 2023. Gold accounted for 8.5 percent of China’s total official reserves at the end of September, compared with 5.5 percent at the end of 2024.

Reserves are assets central banks hold to ensure they can meet international payments and respond to financial disruption. They usually include foreign currencies, foreign government debt and gold.

Private demand for gold within China has also risen, with purchases of gold bars and coins 28.4 percent higher in the first half of 2026 than during the same period last year, according to the China Gold Association. The buying of gold has continued amid falling prices, with gold down around 8.5 percent over the month.

The World Gold Council attributed the decline in gold prices partly to a stronger dollar and higher returns on US government debt. With interest rates going up in an attempt to curb inflation, these investments are attractive for buyers as they pay interest, making them more attractive to private investors than gold, which does not.

A key objective is to reduce dependence on US government debt, known as Treasuries, according to Thu Lan Nguyen, head of commodity research at Commerzbank in Frankfurt.

China holds substantial reserves in dollar-based assets and, therefore, buying gold reduces its exposure to decisions taken in Washington. “China’s gold purchases are part of a broader effort to make its reserves more resilient,” Nguyen told Al Jazeera.

The freezing by Western countries of roughly $300bn in Russian Central Bank overseas assets following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 demonstrated how reserves held abroad can quickly become inaccessible.

The concern for China may be that a future confrontation with Washington could expose some of its overseas assets to similar restrictions. “Gold held domestically has a crucial advantage in this respect: it does not represent a claim on another country and is therefore much less exposed to sanctions or asset freezes,” Nguyen said.

“I would interpret it primarily as risk management,” she added, pointing to increased geopolitical tensions and economic and fiscal risks.

America’s rising debt, which hit $40 trillion for the first time in history earlier this year, adds another source of uncertainty. In February, the US Congressional Budget Office projected that federal debt held by the public would rise from 101 percent of the size of the US economy in 2026 to 120 percent in 2036. That provides context for concerns about Washington’s ability to repay that debt going forward should an economic crash occur. Much of this debt is held by China. Gold, therefore, offers a less volatile and risky asset to hold.

Chinese households have different motivations for buying gold. When confidence in other investments weakens, gold can become more attractive as a way to hold savings. “Strong demand for gold can partly reflect a search for alternative stores of value,” Nguyen said.

The World Gold Council has identified weak Chinese share markets as one factor supporting domestic demand for gold, while its property market is burdened by heavy borrowing and overbuilding, contributing to a fall in housing prices, making it a poorer investment.

Analysts warned that China’s increased buying of gold does not signal an imminent end to the dollar’s global dominance. “I would be cautious about describing this as a major shift away from the dollar,” Nguyen said. “The dollar remains by far the dominant global reserve currency.”

But a gradual shift could still matter if China and other central banks put more of their new reserves into gold, buying fewer US assets than they normally would. That could weaken one source of demand for US government debt. But the effect would depend on how widely and quickly the shift developed.

“The key point is, therefore, that this is likely to be a slow diversification process rather than a sudden abandonment of the dollar,” Nguyen said. She added that the consequences for the US economy would remain limited unless the trend broadened and accelerated substantially.

Central banks also need readily available foreign currency to support international payments and the dollar remains central to those transactions. So gold can provide financial protection, but it cannot directly replace all the functions of dollar reserves.

China is part of a wider trend, particularly among central banks in emerging economies, Nguyen said.

“The trend is particularly visible among emerging market central banks,” Nguyen said. “But sanctions are only part of the story.”

Poland has also become a more prominent buyer. Its central bank purchased 31 tonnes in the first quarter of 2026 and another eight tonnes in July, according to the World Gold Council.

Large holdings do not necessarily indicate recent purchases. India, for example, confirmed in June that its physical gold stock remained unchanged at about 880.5 tonnes. India’s gold reserves have changed little since mid-2025, according to the World Gold Council. It bought about four tonnes in 2025, down from 73 tonnes in 2024.

Despite China’s sustained buying, its reserves remain far smaller than those of the United States. Its holdings of about 2,300 tonnes at the end of 2025 amounted to less than one-third of the US stockpile of approximately 8,133 tonnes.

title: Malaysia’s welcome for Min Aung Hlaing undermines its stand on justice
excerpt:
Executive Director, The Initiative to Promote Tolerance and Prevent Violence (INITIATE.MY).

On October 8, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim received Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing in Putraj...
body_text:
Executive Director, The Initiative to Promote Tolerance and Prevent Violence (INITIATE.MY).

On October 8, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim received Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing in Putrajaya with a guard of honour and an official luncheon, in the military chief’s first visit since the 2021 coup. Nine days earlier, Malaysia sent 1,476 Myanmar nationals back by sea in the first phase of a plan to return 5,000 people.

Kuala Lumpur calls this pragmatic diplomacy. In reality, it lends a middle power’s credibility to the Trump administration’s retreat from international accountability, weakening the laws and institutions smaller states rely on most.

Since May, a surge of online hate speech and misinformation has targeted the Rohingya, Malaysia’s largest refugee community. By late July, at least nine Rohingya community schools had closed or faced closure orders, and more than 100 Rohingya told UNHCR that residents of their Penang village had driven them out.

The hostility ignores the facts: Malaysia’s police chief says Rohingya account for 0.02 percent of crime. Yet research by INITIATE.MY and the Center for the Study of Organized Hate found AI-generated content amplifying anti-Rohingya disinformation across Malaysia, Indonesia, India and Bangladesh, casting refugees as a threat and legitimising vigilante violence.

Electoral politics plays a part. After heavy losses in three state elections, and with a general election due by February 2028, Anwar’s coalition may see a hard line on Rohingya returns as a show of control, though voter disillusionment and right-wing rivals make any electoral gains uncertain.

Malaysia is not acting alone. Mongolia hosted Vladimir Putin in 2024 despite an ICC arrest warrant, and Hungary welcomed Benjamin Netanyahu in 2025 despite another. Kuala Lumpur denies this is recognition, yet Anwar says Malaysia will work towards Myanmar’s full reintegration into ASEAN, and Min Aung Hlaing wants a seat at the bloc’s November summit in Manila. Each welcome makes the next easier and tells leaders accused of atrocities, from Netanyahu to Min Aung Hlaing, that diplomatic rehabilitation is possible without accountability.

ASEAN has tried this before. In April 2021, Min Aung Hlaing agreed to the Five-Point Consensus, then ignored it: The violence continued, the ASEAN special envoy never met Aung San Suu Kyi, and inclusive dialogue never began. The bloc’s one real lever was excluding military leaders from its summits. Myanmar Specialist, Arkar Hein, said “Welcoming him back with nothing asked in return rewards that defiance and tells Naypyidaw that time and a staged election can achieve what
compromise would otherwise require. Each handshake abroad also makes the regime less willing to offer its opponents real concessions, and convinces them that only the battlefield will decide Myanmar’s future.”

Malaysia has spent decades building its credibility as a regional peacemaker, a hard-won reputation it now puts at risk. It has facilitated the Bangsamoro peace process since 2001, helping negotiate a landmark peace agreement in the southern Philippines, and has facilitated talks in southern Thailand since 2013. In November 2024, Anwar welcomed the ICC’s arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his former defence minister, saying they “should be arrested even if they are visiting other countries”. That same month, the ICC prosecutor sought an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing for alleged crimes against humanity targeting the Rohingya, and an Argentinian court has since issued its own.

The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice centres on the 2016-17 operations Min Aung Hlaing commanded, which killed thousands of Rohingya, included mass rapes and burned hundreds of villages, driving more than 700,000 people into Bangladesh. UN investigators called for him to face genocide charges. Malaysia is not a party to the Rome Statute and has no legal duty to arrest him. But its credibility as a peacemaker and on Palestine rests on applying one standard to everyone.

The returns rest on assurances no independent body can verify. UNHCR says it was not involved in the returns and had no access to verify that they were voluntary, and that safe conditions do not exist. Those returned reportedly included 27 children. Though not a party to the Refugee Convention, Malaysia is bound by the customary principle of non-refoulement, and the UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar has warned of substantial risks.

Naypyidaw says no Rohingya are involved because it does not recognise them as citizens, but other returnees also risk arbitrary detention, prosecution and forced recruitment. The military does not even control Rakhine State, where the Arakan Army holds more than 90 percent of the territory. On September 28, a day before returns began, a military air attack reportedly killed at least 50 civilians there, following more than a dozen other mass killings by the military earlier this year.

Nor can the military-backed government deliver the peace that safe return requires. Its election saw no voting in 67 of 330 townships, and when Min Aung Hlaing offered peace talks in April, the National Unity Government (NUG) and major ethnic armed groups refused. Without a ceasefire and an inclusive political process, assurances of safe return ring hollow.

Malaysia’s frustration is nonetheless legitimate. It has hosted refugees for decades with little international support, and resettlement has shrunk since the Trump administration suspended United States refugee admissions in January 2025. But failed burden-sharing cannot justify returns without safeguards.

The ICC exists so that victims of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity can find justice when their own states fail them. That mission now faces unprecedented pressure. On October 9, hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize, the Trump administration sanctioned the court itself. Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Chad and Venezuela have announced their withdrawal.

Yet middle powers can push back. Seventy-nine ICC members, including Canada, Brazil, Mexico and South Africa, backed the court after the first US sanctions in February 2025, and in May Hungary’s new government reversed its predecessor’s withdrawal. In Southeast Asia, the Philippines surrendered former President Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague, and on October 8 judges found him fit to stand trial for crimes against humanity, with proceedings due to begin on November 30.

Middle powers like Malaysia, and blocs such as ASEAN and the European Union, cannot stop US sanctions, but they need not follow the Trump administration’s lead. As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told the World Economic Forum in January, middle powers “must act together, because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu”.

Malaysia and its neighbours should lead by saying no: No to efforts to weaken the court, no to treating Min Aung Hlaing’s presidency as a clean slate, and no to Rohingya returns into an active conflict. Malaysia should back efforts to hold him accountable if ICC judges issue a warrant, and reconsider acceding to the Rome Statute, a move it abandoned in 2019.

Saying no does not mean disengaging. Kuala Lumpur should tie Myanmar’s reintegration into ASEAN to real progress on the Five-Point Consensus, starting with an end to violence and inclusive dialogue involving the NUG and ethnic armed organisations. At home, it should pause returns until an independent body confirms they are safe and voluntary, and hold accountable those who evict, threaten or attack refugees.

Malaysia should not carry this burden alone. ASEAN partners, members of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and donors should fund refugee registration, education and integration, and resettlement countries should restore their commitments. Governments should also hold tech platforms accountable for amplifying anti-refugee disinformation and require swift action against incitement.

For years, Malaysia has offered refuge to the Rohingya and others fleeing Myanmar when few countries would. That record gives it the standing, and the responsibility, to defend the system of international justice it has long championed.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

title: You're probably cooking rice wrong, and chefs reveal the simple mistake to avoid
excerpt: Chef Anthony Vitolo visits the weekend studio to prepare traditional Italian recipes alongside the five hosts. He demonstrates the step-by-step process of breading and frying a classic mozzarella dish...
body_text:
Chef Anthony Vitolo visits the weekend studio to prepare traditional Italian recipes alongside the five hosts. He demonstrates the step-by-step process of breading and frying a classic mozzarella dish, sharing his professional culinary tips. The group gathers around the kitchen table to taste the delicious final creation during this special cooking demonstration.

Rice may be a kitchen staple, but cooking it well at home can be trickier than it seems.

Experts say the trick to tender rice with distinct grains that stay separate instead of clumping together may begin before you even turn on the stove, with a step many home cooks skip.

"I generally rinse before cooking when I want a light, fluffy result," Dennis Littley, a New Jersey-based classically trained chef and founder of Ask Chef Dennis, told Fox News Digital.

FOUR FOODS YOU SHOULD NEVER STORE IN THE FREEZER — AND WHERE TO KEEP THEM INSTEAD

He recommends rinsing long-grain white rice, basmati and jasmine rice until the water goes from very cloudy to mostly clear. It doesn't need to be perfectly transparent, he said.

Rinsing rice before cooking can help remove excess starch and keep the grains from clumping together. (iStock)

The rinse removes some of the loose surface starch that can make rice gummy or clumpy, Littley said. Then, drain it well so the water-to-rice ratio is not thrown off.

But chefs also note that not every type of rice should be treated the same.

CELEBRITY CHEF SAYS IF YOU CAN DRIVE TO MCDONALD'S, YOU CAN COOK HEALTHY MEALS AT HOME

"The important thing is to adjust your technique for the type of rice you're using rather than applying one method to every variety," Littley said.

Chefs recommend rinsing long-grain white rice, basmati and jasmine rice until the water is mostly clear. (iStock)

Christine Pittman, the Florida-based founder and CEO of COOKtheStory, TheCookful and COOKforTWO, said she reserves the rinse for short-grain rice and for when she is cooking rice in a pressure cooker.

Littley and Pittman both suggest skipping the rinse for risotto, noting that the starch helps make the dish creamy.

THE BEST CHEESE FOR A BURGER, ACCORDING TO AN EXPERT — AND WHY SOME POPULAR PICKS FALL FLAT

A recent side-by-side test by Food & Wine found that rinsed and soaked basmati and jasmine rice were lighter and fluffier than unwashed rice, which clumped together. The test combined rinsing and soaking, not rinsing alone.

A few simple tips can help home cooks make rice with tender, separate grains. (iStock)

"I especially like soaking basmati rice for about 20 to 30 minutes before cooking," Littley said. "It helps the grains hydrate evenly and can give you longer, more distinct grains with a nice fluffy texture."

There are other ways home cooks can improve their rice, too.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Pittman recommends a little less than 2 cups of water for every 1 cup of long-grain white rice but says the amount varies by variety. For Japanese-style short-grain white rice, a rough stovetop starting point is 1 1/4 to 1 1/2 cups of water per cup of rice. Littley likewise advises following the package or recipe directions for the specific rice.

While brown rice can also be rinsed, its bran layer means it needs more water — about 2 cups per 1 cup of rice — and more time to cook.

Whether to rinse rice can depend on the variety and how you're cooking it. (iStock)

Briefly toasting rice in a little oil or butter after rinsing and draining, but before adding liquid, can add a nutty flavor and help keep the grains defined, Littley said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Once the rice and cooking liquid are in the pot and the liquid comes to a boil, lower the heat to a gentle simmer and cover the pot, Littley said, and avoid lifting the lid or stirring while it cooks, Littley said. When the rice is done, take it off the heat and let it rest, covered, for five to 10 minutes before fluffing with a fork. Letting it rest allows moisture to redistribute for a more even texture.

"Overcooked rice is bad, but my hot take is that undercooked rice is worse."

Once the rice and cooking liquid are in the pot and the liquid comes to a boil, lower the heat to a gentle simmer, cover the pot and avoid lifting the lid or stirring while it cooks, Littley said. When the rice is done, take it off the heat and let it rest, covered, for five to 10 minutes before fluffing with a fork. Letting it rest allows moisture to redistribute for a more even texture.

For Pittman, the fluffing step is also crucial to good rice. She recommends fluffing it with a dinner fork, using a "gentle folding motion" to lift the rice from the bottom of the pot rather than stirring it vigorously.

"You're really only touching the bottom of the rice with your fork, and the rest of the rice on top is moving sort of like a little avalanche from the pressure of the fork underneath," she said.

Experts recommend gently folding rice with a fork when mixing to keep the grains intact. (iStock)

If it's undercooked, Pittman said, add a little hot water, cover the pot and return it to low heat.

"Overcooked rice is bad, but my hot take is that undercooked rice is worse," she said.

Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: US in ‘denuclearisation’ talks with Russia and China: Trump
excerpt:
The United States is engaged in talks with Russia and China regarding nuclear disarmament, President Donald Trump has announced.

Trump said on Thursday that China – which lags behind the US and Russi...
body_text:
The United States is engaged in talks with Russia and China regarding nuclear disarmament, President Donald Trump has announced.

Trump said on Thursday that China – which lags behind the US and Russia in terms of the number of warheads it has – is racing to catch up. He added during an interview with US broadcaster Newsmax that Washington is discussing with its peers a route to “denuclearise”.

China’s nuclear stockpile of about 620 warheads is dwarfed by those of the US and Russia, which each have more than 4,000, but Trump said he thinks China will “catch up” within five years.

“The whole thing is a shame because I’d love to denuclearise if possible,” Trump said. “We’re actually talking ⁠to Russia about that, and ⁠we’re talking to China about that denuclearisation.”

China doesn’t seem willing to disarm, he noted, but said talks have continued. Newsmax reported that Trump spoke with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the subject, but no further details regarding the talks with either Russia or China were revealed.

Russia has the world’s largest stockpile of nuclear warheads, and the US is close behind, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).

The two countries together possess an estimated 86 percent of all nuclear weapons globally.

China has the third largest nuclear arsenal, according to SIPRI, having expanded it to 620 warheads in the past year.

Trump’s claims came shortly after the expiration of the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, an arms control agreement between the US and Russia to limit their nuclear arsenals.

A month after the treaty expired, French President Emmanuel Macron announced the Forward Deterrence Initiative as Russia’s nuclear sabre-rattling during its war on Ukraine has spooked Europe.

Former Australian Minister of Foreign Affairs Gareth Evans told Al Jazeera that the world’s interest in the risk of nuclear weapons has waned.

“[The] world … has become alarmingly complacent about the risks of nuclear war with every major nuclear arms control agreement dead, dying or on life support and the longstanding taboo against threat or use eroding,” he said
